semin-durr:5-5.t:
His saying, Exalted is He: {اليوم أُحِلَّ لَكُمُ}: the discussion of it is like the discussion of what precedes it. Some people claimed that what is meant by the three "days" (اليوم) mentioned here is a single time, and that He repeated it only for tawkīd (emphasis), and that because of the differing events that occurred in it the repetition was fitting; but this is nothing. Some claimed that there is a fronting and a postponement in the speech, and that the original order is: «فاذكروا اسم اللهِ عليه وكلُوا مِمَّا أَمْسَكْن عليكم»; this resembles the view of those who make the pronoun refer back to the hunting animals that are sent out.

His saying: {وَطَعَامُ الذين}: there are two views on it. The correct one of them is that it is a mubtadaʾ (subject), and its khabar (predicate) is «حِلُّ لكم». He brought out the statement of this in a nominal clause out of concern for the question that was asked about it. Abū al-Baqāʾ permitted that it be nominative (marfūʿ) by conjunction with the nominative noun whose agent is not named, namely «الطيبات», and he made His saying «حِلٌّ لكم» the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ. This ought not to be permitted at all, because it supposes something that is not needed, together with the loss of the eloquence of the speech. His saying: {وَطَعَامُكُمْ حِلٌّ لَّهُمْ} is a mubtadaʾ and khabar; and by analogy with Abū al-Baqāʾ's view, «طعام» would be conjoined to what precedes it and «حِلٌّ» the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ — but he did not mention this, as though he sensed what is correct.

His saying: {والمحصنات}: there are likewise two views on its nominative case. One of them: that it is a mubtadaʾ whose khabar is omitted, i.e. "the chaste women are also lawful for you"; this is the apparent view. Abū al-Baqāʾ chose that it be conjoined to «الطيبات», for he said: «مِن المؤمنات» is a ḥāl (circumstantial) from the pronoun in «المُحْصَنات», or from «المحصنات» itself if you conjoin it to «الطيبات»; and «حِلٌّ» is a maṣdar (verbal noun) in the sense of the participle, which is why it is not made feminine, dual or plural, since that is the better of the two usages for maṣdars that occur as descriptions of concrete things. In the rhyming echo-form (al-itbāʿ) one says: «حِلُّ بِلُّ», which is like their saying «حَسَن بَسَن» and «عَطْشان نَطْشان». And «من المؤمنات» is a ḥāl, as has preceded: either from the pronoun in «المحصنات» or from «المحصنات» itself. The discussion of the derivation of this word and of the readers' differences over it has already preceded in Sūrat al-Nisāʾ.

His saying: {إِذَآ آتَيْتُمُوهُنَّ}: an adverb (ẓarf), governed by one of two things: either «أُحِلَّ» or the omitted «حِلُّ», according to what has been established. The clause after it is in the position of the genitive by its being annexed to it, and here it is for mere time-reference. It may also be conditional with its apodosis (jawāb al-sharṭ) omitted, i.e. "when you have given them their dowries, they become lawful for you"; the first is more apparent. And «مُحْصِنين» is a ḥāl, governed by one of three things: either «آتيتموهُنَّ», the owner of the ḥāl being the nominative pronoun; or «أُحِلَّ», which is passive; or the omitted «حِلٌّ», as has preceded. As for «غيرَ», three views are permissible in it. One: that it is accusative (manṣūb) as a naʿt (adjective) of «محصنين». The second: that it may be accusative as a ḥāl, the owner of the ḥāl being the latent (mustatir) pronoun in «مُحْصِنين». The third: that it is a ḥāl from the agent of «آتيتموهن», as a second ḥāl from it, according to those who permit that. His saying: {وَلاَ متخذي}: it may be genitive (majrūr) by conjunction with «مسافحين», «لا» being added to emphasise the negation understood from «غير»; and accusative by conjunction with «غير» according to its three views. It is not permissible to conjoin it to «مُحْصِنين», because it is accompanied by «لا», which emphasises a preceding negation, and there is no negation with «محصنين». The meanings of these words have already preceded.

His saying: {وَمَن يَكْفُرْ بالإيمان}: its parallels have already preceded. It was said: what is meant by "faith" (الإيمان) is that which is believed in, so it is a maṣdar standing in the place of the object, like «درهم ضَرْبُ الأمير» ("a dirham of the prince's minting"). It was also said: there is an omitted muḍāf there, i.e. "in the One Who necessitates faith", namely the Creator, Blessed and Exalted is He.

His saying: {وَهُوَ فِي الآخرة مِنَ الخاسرين}: the apparent view is that the khabar is His saying «من الخاسرين», so His saying «في الآخرة» is attached to (mutaʿalliq) what this khabar is attached to. Makkī said: "What governs the adverb is omitted, its implied form being: «وهو خاسر في الآخرةِ», and His saying «من الخاسرين» indicates the omitted element. If you make the alif and lām in «الخاسرين» not in the sense of «الذين», it is permissible for what governs the adverb to be «من الخاسرين»." He means that if it were a relative, it would be impossible for what comes after it to govern what precedes it, because nothing within the domain of a relative may come before it; this is as they said about His saying: {إِنِّي لِعَمَلِكُمْ مِّنَ القالين} [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 168] and {وَكَانُواْ فِيهِ مِنَ الزاهدين} [Yūsuf: 20]. Makkī's supposition of what this adverb is attached to, namely «خاسر», is based only on «أل» being a relative, as shown by his saying: "If you make the alif and lām not in the sense of «الذين»". In any case there is no need for this supposition; rather what governs it, as has preceded, is what governs the adverb that occurs as a khabar, namely general existence (al-kawn al-muṭlaq). It is not permissible for «في الآخرة» to be the khabar and «من الخاسرين» to be attached to what it is attached to, because there would be no benefit in that. If «من الخاسرين» is made a ḥāl from the pronoun of the khabar, being a permanent ḥāl, that is permissible, but it is weak in i'rab. This has preceded, and the parallel of this verse has preceded in al-Baqara at His saying: {وَإِنَّهُ فِي الآخرة لَمِنَ الصالحين} [verse 130].

semin-durr:99-99.t: His saying, Exalted is He: {إِلاَّ البلاغ}: there are two views on its being nominative (marfūʿ). The first: it is the fāʿil (agent) of the preposition-and-genitive phrase before it, because that phrase relies on the negation, i.e. "nothing is incumbent upon the Messenger except the conveying." The second: it is a mubtadaʾ (subject), and its khabar (predicate) is the preposition-and-genitive phrase before it. On both analyses the exception is mufarragh (an exception whose excepted-from term is left unexpressed).

semin-durr:100-100.t:
His saying, Exalted is He: {وَلَوْ أَعْجَبَكَ كَثْرَةُ}: its apodosis (jawāb al-sharṭ) is omitted, i.e. "and even if the abundance of the bad should impress you, it would not be equal to the good," or: "it would avail nothing toward equality."

And «البلاغ» may be a maṣdar (verbal noun) of «بَلَّغ» with the doubled consonant, i.e. "nothing is upon him except the conveying (التبليغ)," so that it came with the augment letters dropped, like «نبات» after «أنبت». And it may be a maṣdar of «بَلَغ» without doubling, in the sense of «البلوغ» (reaching), the meaning being: "nothing is upon him except reaching [them] through his conveying it"; for reaching is a necessary consequence [of conveying], so the consequence was used to express what entails it.
[Translator's note: the paragraph on «البلاغ» concerns verse 99 ({مَّا عَلَى الرسول إِلاَّ البلاغ}), but it stands in the source under this entry, and is translated here as written.]

semin-durr:104-104.t:
His saying, Exalted is He: {حَسْبُنَا مَا وَجَدْنَا عَلَيْهِ آبَاءَنَآ}: «حسبنا» is a mubtadaʾ (subject). It has been stated earlier that it is originally a maṣdar (verbal noun), and what is meant by it is the active participle, i.e. "sufficient for us" (كافينا); Ibn ʿAṭiyya's explanation of it as «كفانا» ("it suffices us") is an explanation of meaning, not of i'rab. And «ما وَجَدْنا» is the khabar (predicate). The apparent sense of «ما» is that it is a nominal relative noun, and it may be an indefinite noun qualified by an adjective, i.e. "sufficient for us is that which we found." And «وجد» may be in the sense of coming upon (encountering), in which case «عليه» admits two views. The first: it is attached to (mutaʿalliq) «وجدنا», and the verb is transitive to one object. The second: it is a ḥāl (circumstantial) from «آباءنا», i.e. "we found them settled upon it." And it may be in the sense of knowing, in which case it is transitive to two objects, the second of them being «عليه».

And His saying: {أَوَلَوْ كَانَ}: the i'rab of this was given earlier in al-Baqara, together with what was said about it: that «لو» here has the meaning of condition and that the wāw is circumstantial (wāw al-ḥāl). The explanation of all of that was given earlier, which makes repeating it unnecessary; except that Ibn ʿAṭiyya said here: "The alif of tawqīf (pausing, i.e. making the hearer stop and take note) has entered upon the wāw of conjunction." I say: Calling this hamza "of tawqīf" is a terminological oddity. Al-Zamakhsharī made this wāw circumstantial, whereas Ibn ʿAṭiyya made it conjunctive, and the reconciliation of their two statements was given earlier in al-Baqara, so do turn your attention to it. The difference in wording between these two verses — I mean the verse of al-Baqara and the verse of al-Māʾida — such as His saying there «اتبعوا» and here «تعالَوْا», and there «أَلْفَيْنا» and here «وجدنا», belongs to the category of variation (tafannun) in eloquence, so no special correspondence should be sought for it; even though I did take pains over that and transmitted it from people in the book "al-Tafsīr al-Kabīr".

semin-durr:102-102.t:
His saying, Exalted is He: {قَدْ سَأَلَهَا}: the pronoun in «سألها» apparently refers back to «أشياء». But al-Zamakhsharī said: "If you say: how did He say 'do not ask about things' and then say «قد سَألَها» and not 'asked about them' (سألَ عنها)? I say: [the pronoun in «سألها»] does not refer back to «أشياء» such that it would be made transitive to it by «عن»; rather it refers back to the question (المسألة) indicated by His saying «لا تَسْألوا», i.e. a people asked the question, then became disbelievers by it — i.e. by what it led to." Ibn ʿAṭiyya followed his approach. The Shaykh [Abū Ḥayyān] said: "Their statement is only tenable with the omission of a muḍāf, and some exegetes stated it explicitly, i.e. 'asked the like of it,' i.e. the like of this question, or the like of these questions."

And al-Ḥawfī said about «سألها»: "The apparent sense is that the pronoun refers back to «أشياء», but taking it according to its apparent sense is untenable, neither from the side of Arabic wording nor from the side of meaning. As for the side of wording: it ought to have been made transitive by «عن», as it was made transitive in the first instance. As for the side of meaning: the thing asked about is decisively different, for their asking is other than the asking of those before them. The asking of these people was like one who asked: 'Where is my she-camel?', 'What is in my she-camel's belly?', 'Where is my father?' and 'Where will I enter?' And the asking of those [earlier people] was other than this, such as: {أَنزِلْ عَلَيْنَا مَآئِدَةً} [al-Māʾida: 114], {أَرِنَا الله جَهْرَةً} [al-Nisāʾ: 153], {اجعل لَّنَآ إلها} [al-Aʿrāf: 138] and the like."
[Translator's note: the source reads «وأين أبي» ("where is my father"); in the well-known reports the question was "who is my father?".]

And al-Wāḥidī said, transmitting from al-Jurjānī: "This asking in the verses differs from the meaning of asking in His saying {لاَ تَسْأَلُواْ عَنْ أَشْيَآءَ} {وَإِن تَسْأَلُواْ عَنْهَا}. Do you not see that the asking in the first verse was made transitive by the preposition, while here it was not made transitive by the preposition? That is because the asking here is a request for the thing itself, as in «سَأَلْتُك درهماً» ('I asked you for a dirham'), i.e. I requested it from you; whereas the asking in the first verse is an asking about the state of the thing and its manner. He only conjoined His saying {قَدْ سَأَلَهَا قَوْمٌ} to what precedes it, although it is not like it in interpretation, because He was forbidding them from burdening themselves with what they had not been charged with, and which had been lifted from them."

I say: it may refer back to «أشياء» in wording, not in meaning, just as the grammarians said in the case of «عندي درهمٌ ونصفُه» ("I have a dirham and half of it"), i.e. and half of another dirham. And of this kind is:
181 - 4- وكلُّ أُناسٍ قاربوا قَيْدَ فَحْلِهِمْ ... ونحنُ خَلَعْنا قيدَه فَهْوَ سارِبُ
(Every people kept their stallion's tether short, but we cast off its tether, so it roams free.)

His saying: {مِّن قَبْلِكُم} is attached to (mutaʿalliq) His saying {سَأَلَهَا}. If it is said: may it be a naʿt (adjective) of «قوم»? I say: a group prohibited that, giving as their reason that an adverb of time does not occur as a khabar (predicate), a naʿt or a ḥāl (circumstantial) of a concrete entity (al-jutha). Something like this was given to you earlier at the beginning of al-Baqara, at His saying {والذين مِن قَبْلِكُمْ} [verse 21], for the ṣila (relative clause) is like the naʿt. And «بها» is attached to «كافرين»; it was only placed first for the sake of the verse-endings (al-fawāṣil).

And al-Nakhaʿī read «سالها» with imāla (inclination of the vowel) and without hamza; these are two dialects, and from this is «يَتَساولان». His applying imāla to «سأل» is like Ḥamza's imāla of «خاف». The verification of that was given earlier in al-Baqara at {فَإِنَّ لَكُمْ مَّا سَأَلْتُمْ} [verse 61] and {سَلْ بني إِسْرَائِيلَ} [verse 211].

semin-durr:38-38.t:
His saying, Exalted is He: {والسارق والسارقة}: the majority read it with the nominative (rafʿ), while ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar and Ibn Abī ʿAbla read it with the accusative (naṣb). It is transmitted from Ubayy: «والسُّرَّقُ والسُّرَّقةُ», with a ḍamma on the sīn and a fatḥa on the rāʾ, both doubled. al-Khaffāf said: "I found it so in the codex of Ubayy." Among those who vocalised them as I have mentioned is Abū ʿAmr. However, Ibn ʿAṭiyya considered this reading a scribal misreading (taṣḥīf), for he said: "It seems likely that this is a misreading on the part of the one who vocalised it, because the reading of the community, when «والسارق» is written without an alif, agrees with this one in the script." I say: this reading can be accounted for in an evident way, namely that السُّرَّق is the plural of سارق, for the pattern فُعَّل is regularly used as the plural of the pattern فاعل when it is an adjective, as in ضارب and ضُرَّب. The proof that the plural is intended is the reading of ʿAbd Allāh [ibn Masʿūd]: «والسارقون والسارقات», with the two sound-plural forms, which shows that the plural is intended. Yet one thing in this is problematic for us: the pattern فُعَّل is the plural of both فاعِل and فاعِلة; one says «نساء ضُرَّب» (women who strike) just as one says «رجالٌ ضُرَّب» (men who strike), and they do not attach the feminine tāʾ to it when females are meant. Here, however, السُّرَّقة in this reading — as you have seen — carries the feminine tāʾ where فُعَّل is meant as the plural of فاعِلة, so it is problematic from this angle. It cannot be said that this tāʾ may be there to reinforce the plural, because that is something preserved from usage and not used as a basis for analogy, as in «حِجارة» (stones).

As for the reading of the majority, there are two views on it. The first — the doctrine of Sībawayh and the best-known of the views of the Basrans — is that «السارقُ» is a mubtadaʾ (subject) whose khabar (predicate) is omitted, its implied form being: "Among what is recited to you — or: among what has been prescribed — is [the case of] the thief, male and female," i.e. the ruling on the thief. His saying «فاقْطَعُوا» is then an explanation of that implied ruling, so what comes after the fāʾ is linked to what precedes it; that is why the fāʾ was brought in it, because it is what is intended, and the fāʾ was not omitted lest it be thought to be unrelated. On this view the speech consists of two sentences: the first declarative, the second imperative. The second view — the doctrine of al-Akhfash, also transmitted from al-Mubarrad and a large group — is that it is likewise a mubtadaʾ, and the khabar is the imperative clause {فاقطعوا}. The fāʾ entered the khabar only because it resembles a conditional, since the alif and lām in it are a relative (mawṣūl) meaning «الذي» and «التي», and the adjective is its ṣila (relative clause); it is thus equivalent to saying: "And the man who stole and the woman who stole — cut off …". al-Zamakhsharī allowed both views; he attributed the first to Sībawayh and did not attribute the second, but said: "Another view is that both are nominative as mubtadaʾ, and the khabar is «فاقطعوا»."

Sībawayh chose the view that its khabar is omitted — as its implied form was given above — rather than the request clause after it, for two reasons. The first: the accusative is the proper construction in such a case in the speech of the Arabs, as in «زيداً فاضربه» (Zayd — strike him), because of the imperative after it. Sībawayh said about this verse: "The proper construction in the speech of the Arabs is the accusative, as you say «زيداً فاضربه», but the generality [of readers] insisted on nothing but the nominative." The second: the entry of the fāʾ into its khabar. In his view the fāʾ enters only into the khabar of an explicit relative such as «الذي» and «مَنْ», under further conditions which I have mentioned in my books on grammar. That is because the fāʾ enters only because the mubtadaʾ resembles a conditional, and they stipulated that its ṣila be fit for a conditional particle, by being a verbal clause with future meaning, or what stands in its place such as an adverb and the like. Hence, when it is not fit for a conditional particle, the fāʾ may not enter the khabar. The ṣila of «أل» is not fit to follow a conditional particle directly, so the fāʾ does not enter its khabar. Moreover, «أل» together with its ṣila counts as a single noun, which is why the case-inflection passes beyond it [onto the ṣila].

As for the reading of ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar and Ibrāhīm [ibn Abī ʿAbla], the accusative is by a concealed verb interpreted by the governor acting on what is connected to the two of them, as in «زيداً فأكرم أخاه» (Zayd — honour his brother). The implied form is: "So punish the male thief and the female thief." You assume a verb from its meaning, as in «زيداً ضربْتُ غلامه» (Zayd — I struck his servant), i.e. "I humiliated Zayd." It is also possible to assume a governor agreeing in wording, since it is acceptable to say «قطعت السارق» (I cut the thief). This reading is clear because of the imperative after the noun from which [the verb] is diverted (ishtighāl).

al-Zamakhsharī said: "Sībawayh preferred it over the reading of the generality because of the imperative, since «زيداً فاضربه» is better than «زيدٌ فاضربه»." His report that [Sībawayh] preferred the accusative over the reading of the generality is open to question, and this becomes clear from Sībawayh's own text. Sībawayh said: "The proper construction in the speech of the Arabs is the accusative, as you say «زيداً اضربه», but the generality insisted on nothing but the nominative." There is nothing in this that entails preferring the accusative; rather, the meaning of his words is that this verse has nothing to do with ishtighāl (diversion of the governor), since if it were of the ishtighāl type the proper construction would have been the accusative; but the majority read it only with the nominative, which shows that the verse is to be construed as two utterances, as stated above, not as one utterance. This is evident.

al-Fakhr al-Rāzī refuted Sībawayh in five ways, because he understood a preference for the accusative, just as the author of al-Kashshāf understood. al-Fakhr al-Rāzī said: "What Sībawayh held is worthless, and several points show its corruption. First: it is an attack on a mass-transmitted (mutawātir) reading transmitted from the Messenger and from the leading figures of the community, and that is definitely false. If Sībawayh were to say: 'I do not say the reading with the nominative is impermissible; I only say the reading with the accusative is preferable,' we say: this too is bad, because preferring a reading read by no one but ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar over the reading of the Messenger and the whole community in the age of the Companions and the Successors is something objectionable and a rejected statement. Second: if the reading with the accusative were preferable, there would necessarily be among the readers someone who read {واللذان يأتيانِها منكم فآذوهما} with the accusative; since no one among the readers is found to read it so, we know that this view falls. Third: if we make «السارق والسارقة» a mubtadaʾ whose khabar is concealed, namely what he assumes as 'among what is recited to you', there remains something else to which the fāʾ in His saying {فاقطعوا} is connected. If he says: the fāʾ is connected to the verb indicated by His saying «والسارق والسارقة», meaning that when he commits theft, cut off his hand, we say: if in the end you need [to say] that «السارق والسارقة» [has the implied form] 'whoever steals', then state this from the outset so that you do not need the concealment you mentioned. Fourth: if we choose the reading with the accusative, it does not indicate that theft is the cause ('illa) of the obligation of cutting, whereas if we choose the reading with the nominative, the verse conveys this meaning; and this meaning is then reinforced by His saying {جَزَآءً بِمَا كَسَبَا}. So it is established that the reading with the nominative is preferable. Fifth: Sībawayh said: 'They put first what is more important and what they are more concerned to make clear.' The reading with the nominative entails mentioning his being a thief before mentioning the obligation of cutting, and this entails that the greatest concern is directed to explaining what relates to the state of the thief qua thief; whereas the reading with the accusative entails that the concern to explain the cutting is greater than the concern with his being a thief. It is known that this is not so, for what is intended in this verse is to denounce theft and to deter from it emphatically. So it is established that the reading with the nominative is the one that must be adopted." End of what he claimed to be a refutation of the imam of the craft.

The answer to the first point is what was given above in reply to what al-Zamakhsharī said, and it has already been given. It is supported by Sībawayh's text, for he said: "«عبدُ الله فاضربه» may be good and sound when it is built on a mubtadaʾ, overt or concealed. As for the overt, it is his saying «هذا زيدٌ فاضرِبْه» (this is Zayd, so strike him). If you wish, «هذا» is not expressed and it functions as it does when overt; that is your saying «الهلالُ واللَّهِ فانظرْ إليه» (the new moon, by Allah — look at it), as though you had said «هذا الهلال» and then brought the imperative. Of this kind is the poet's saying:

1725 - وقائلةٍ: خَوْلانُ فانكِحْ فتاتَهُمْ ... وأُكْرومةُ الحَيَّيْنِ خِلْوٌ كما هِيا
(Many a woman saying: "[These are] Khawlān, so marry their girl" — while the noblest of the two clans is still unmarried, as she was.)

It was heard thus from the Arabs reciting it," meaning with «خولان» in the nominative. So given his saying "may be good and sound," how [can he be] attacking the nominative? As for his saying "If Sībawayh were to say … to the end," Sībawayh does not say that — how could he say it when he has given preference to the nominative in the way I have made clear? His saying "read by no one but ʿĪsā" is not as he claimed; rather, a group read it, such as Ibrāhīm ibn Abī ʿAbla. Furthermore, these did not read it of their own accord; rather, they transmitted it in a chain reaching the Messenger ﷺ. The most that can be said is that it is not as well known as the first.

To the second: Sībawayh did not claim that the accusative is preferable so that he should be bound by what [al-Rāzī] said; rather, he construed the reading of the generality as two sentences, for the reason I mentioned to you above concerning the entry of the fāʾ. That is why, when Sībawayh gave examples of the imperative and prohibitive sentence after the noun, he gave them devoid of the fāʾ; he said: "That is your saying «زيداً اضربْه» and «وعمراً امرُرْ به»."

To the third: what was stated above about the wisdom requiring the bringing of the fāʾ, and its being a link connecting the ruling to what precedes it.

To the fourth: by denying that there is a difference between the nominative and the accusative in that the nominative entails the cause and the accusative does not. That is because the verse is of the type of giving the cause by means of the attribute on which the ruling is based. Do you not see that your saying «اقطع السارق» (cut off the thief) conveys the cause, i.e. that it makes his being characterised by theft the cause of the cutting? So this indicates the cause even with the accusative explicitly used.

To the fifth: they put first what is more important where the predicative relation differs, as with the agent and the object. Let us quote Sībawayh's text so that what we have mentioned becomes clear. Sībawayh said: "If you put [the object] first and the agent last, the wording runs as it did in the first" — meaning in «ضرب عبدُ الله زيداً» (ʿAbd Allāh struck Zayd). He said: "That is: «ضرب زيداً عبدُ الله», because you intend by it, when put last, what you intend by it when put first, and you did not intend the verb to be occupied with what comes before it, even if it is put last in the wording. Hence the proper rule of the wording is that it should be put first in it, and it is good Arabic and frequent; it is as though they put first that whose explanation is more important to them and which they are more concerned to make clear, even if both are of importance and concern to them." The noble verse is not of this kind.

His saying: {أَيْدِيَهُمَا}: a plural standing in the place of the dual because there is no risk of ambiguity, since it is known that from each thief his right hand is cut. It is of the type of {صَغَتْ قُلُوبُكُمَا} [al-Taḥrīm: 4]. This is indicated by the reading of ʿAbd Allāh: «فاقطعوا أيمانَهما» (cut off their right hands). The grammarians stipulated conditions for the plural standing in the place of the dual, among them: that the part annexed be single in its owner, as in «قلوبكما» (your [two] hearts) and «رؤوس الكبشين» (the heads of the two rams), because there is no risk of confusion — unlike the eyes, the hands and the feet. If you said «فَقَأْتُ أعينَهما» (I gouged out their eyes) meaning their two eyes [one each], or «كَتَّفْتُ أيديَهما» (I tied their hands) meaning their two hands [one each], it would not be permissible because of the ambiguity. Were it not that the evidence shows that what is meant is the two right hands, this would not have been acceptable. This — I mean the plural standing in the place of the dual under its conditions — is widespread in their language. The Exalted said: {فَقَدْ صَغَتْ قُلُوبُكُمَا} [al-Taḥrīm: 4].

Let us state the question, and we say: any two parts that are annexed to their two wholes, in wording or by implication, and that are each single in their owners, admit three options. The best is the plural; next comes the singular according to some of them, and next the dual. Others said: the best is the plural, then the dual, then the singular; e.g. «قَطَعْتُ رؤوسَ الكبشين» , «ورأسَ الكبشين» and «ورأسَيْ الكبشين» (I cut off the heads / the head / the two heads of the two rams). [The poet] said:

1726 - ومَهْمَهَيْنِ قَذَفَيْنِ مَرْتَيْنْ ... ظهراهُما مثلُ ظهورِ التُّرْسَيْنْ
(And two remote, barren wastelands, whose two backs [surfaces] are like the backs of two shields.)

My saying "two parts" is a precaution against two separate things: if you said «قبضت دراهمكما» meaning «دِرْهميكما» (I received your two dirhams), it would not be permissible because of ambiguity; but if [ambiguity] is safe, it is permissible, as in his saying «اضرباه بأسيافِكما» (strike him with your swords) and «إلى مضاجعكما» (to your resting places). Our saying "annexed" is a precaution against their being separated, as in His saying {على لِسَانِ دَاوُودَ وَعِيسَى ابن مَرْيَمَ} [al-Māʾida: 78]. Our saying "in wording," its example is: [the above], for the annexation in it is in the wording. [Translator's note: the example after «مثالُه» appears to be missing in the source text.] Our saying "or by implication," as in his saying:

1727 - رأيت بني البكري في حومة الوغى ... كاغِرَي الأفواهِ عند عَرِين
(I saw the sons of al-Bakrī in the thick of battle like two [beasts] with gaping mouths at a lair.)

For its implied form is «كفاغري أفواههما» (like two gaping their mouths). [Translator's note: the source prints «كاغِرَي» in the verse and «أفواهما» in the explanation; the intended forms appear to be «كفاغِرَي» and «أفواههما».] Our saying "single" is a precaution against the eyes and the like. The plural was preferred over the dual, even though [the dual] is the original, because of the heaviness of two successive duals; and the plural was preferable to the singular because it shares with the dual in combining [more than one]; after it comes the singular, because there is no heaviness. This is according to some of them, who said: "because the dual occurs only out of poetic necessity, as in his saying:

1728 - هما نَفَثا في فِيَّ مِنْ فَمَوَيْهِما ... على النابحِ العاوي أشدَّ رِجامِ
(The two of them blew into my mouth from their two mouths, against the barking, howling one, the most violent of stonings [i.e. invective].)

— unlike the singular, which has occurred in eloquent speech, including: «مَسَح أذنيه ظاهرَهما وباطنَهما» (he wiped his two ears, their outside and their inside)." Others said: "The best is the plural, then the dual, then the singular, as in his saying:

1729 - حمامةَ بطنِ الواديَيْن تَرَنَّمي ... سَقاكِ من الغُرِّ الغوادِي مطيرُها
(O dove of the hollow of the two valleys, coo! May the rain-laden of the white morning clouds water you.)"

al-Zamakhsharī said: "«أيديهما» means «يديهما» (their two hands); similar is {فَقَدْ صَغَتْ قُلُوبُكُمَا} [al-Taḥrīm: 4]: the dual of the muḍāf ilayhi was considered sufficient in place of the dual of the muḍāf. By the two hands the two right hands are meant, as is indicated by the reading of ʿAbd Allāh: «والسارقون والسارقات فاقطعوا أَيْمانهم»." The Shaykh [Abū Ḥayyān] objected to him that the two are not alike: in the first type the use of the plural in place of the dual is regular, unlike the second, which is not subject to analogy, because what first comes to mind from your saying «قَطَعْتُ آذانَ الزيدين» (I cut off the ears of the two Zayds) is four ears. This objection is worthless, because the evidence shows that what is meant is the two right hands.

His saying: {جَزَآءً}: there are four views on it. First: it is accusative as a maṣdar (verbal noun) by an implied verb, i.e. «جازوهما جزاءً» (requite them both with a requital). Second: it is also a maṣdar, but accusative in the sense of a kind of the maṣdar, because His saying «فاقطعوا» is equivalent to "requite them both by cutting off the hands, as a requital." Third: it is accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial). This ḥāl may be from the agent, i.e. "requiting them both by cutting because of what they earned," or from the muḍāf ilayhi in «أيديهما», i.e. "in the state of their being requited." The ḥāl may come from the muḍāf ilayhi because the muḍāf is part of it, as in His saying {وَنَزَعْنَا مَا فِي صُدُورِهِم مِّنْ غِلٍّ إِخْوَاناً} [al-Ḥijr: 47]. Fourth: it is a mafʿūl li-ajlihi (object of purpose), i.e. for the sake of requital, and the conditions for the accusative are present.

«نَكالاً» is accusative just as «جزاء» is accusative. al-Zamakhsharī mentioned nothing for the two of them but the mafʿūl li-ajlihi. The Shaykh said: "He followed al-Zajjāj in that." Then he said: "It is not good, unless the requital is itself the exemplary punishment, in which case it would be by way of badal (substitute); but if the two are distinct, that is not permissible except by means of a conjunction." I say: exemplary punishment (nakāl) is a kind of requital, so it is a badal of it. [Moreover, what ought to be said here is that «جزاء» is a mafʿūl li-ajlihi, governed by] «فاقطعوا», so the requital is the cause of the command to cut; and «نَكالاً» is also a mafʿūl li-ajlihi governed by «جزاء», and the exemplary punishment is the cause of the requital. So the cause is itself explained by another cause, and it is like the nested ḥāl (al-ḥāl al-mutadākhila), as you say «ضربته تأديباً له إحساناً إليه» (I struck him to discipline him, as a kindness to him): the discipline is the cause of the striking and the kindness the cause of the discipline. The words of al-Zamakhsharī, and of al-Zajjāj before him, do not contradict what I have mentioned, for there is no contradiction between this and their saying that «جزاء» is a mafʿūl li-ajlihi, and likewise «نكالاً». Reflect on it, for it is a good view. Thus the objection against al-Zamakhsharī and al-Zajjāj falls away, as does the distinction drawn in his saying "unless the requital is itself the exemplary punishment." Afterwards I came upon [evidence] that the mafʿūl lahu may govern in the accusative another mafʿūl lahu [that is a cause] for it. For the parsers allowed, in His saying {أَن يَكْفُرُواْ بِمَآ أنَزَلَ الله بَغْياً} [al-Baqara: 90], that «بغياً» be a mafʿūl lahu, and then they mentioned regarding His saying «أَنْ يُنَزِّل الله» that it is a mafʿūl lahu governed by «بغياً», so it is a cause of it. They stated this explicitly, so what I said has become clear.

«بما» is attached to «جزاء». «ما» may be maṣdariyya, i.e. "for their earning," or it may mean «الذي», with the returning pronoun omitted because the conditions are complete, i.e. "for what they earned." The bāʾ is causal.

semin-durr:6-6.t:
His saying, Exalted is He: {إِذَا قُمْتُمْ إِلَى الصلاة}: they said its implied meaning is: "when you intend to stand", like His saying: {فَإِذَا قَرَأْتَ القرآن فاستعذ} [al-Naḥl: 98]. This is putting the effect in the place of the cause, for standing is caused by intention, and intention is its cause.

Al-Zamakhsharī said: "If you say: why is it permissible to express the intention of the act by the act? I say: because the act comes into existence through the agent's ability to do it and his intention for it, which is his aiming at it, his inclination and the purity of his motive. Just as the ability to do an act is expressed by the act in their saying 'man does not fly, and the blind man does not see', i.e. they are not able to fly and to see — and of this is His saying, Exalted is He: {نُّعِيدُهُ وَعْداً عَلَيْنَآ إِنَّا كُنَّا فَاعِلِينَ} [al-Anbiyāʾ: 104], i.e. able to restore it — likewise the intention of the act is expressed by the act. That is because the act is caused by the ability, so the effect is put in the place of the cause because of the connection between them and for the concision of the speech." It was also said: its implied meaning is "when you head for the prayer", because whoever turns towards something and rises to it is heading for it, so heading was expressed by standing. The majority supposed an omitted ḥāl (circumstantial) from the agent of «قمتم», i.e. "when you rise to the prayer in a state of ritual impurity (muḥdithīn)", since there is no ablution required of one who is not ritually impure — although a group held that view. They said: what indicates this omitted ḥāl is its being set against His saying: {وَإِن كُنتُمْ جُنُباً فاطهروا}, as though it were said: "if you are in the state of minor impurity, wash such-and-such and wipe such-and-such, and if you are in the state of major impurity, wash the whole body". This is open to consideration.

His saying: {إِلَى المرافق}: there are two views on this «إلى». One of them: that it has its proper sense of the end-point of the extent; and in that case there is disagreement over it. One says that what comes after it does not enter into what comes before it; one says the reverse of that; one says that it has nothing to say about inclusion or non-inclusion, and that inclusion and exclusion turn only on the presence or absence of evidence; one says that if what comes after it is of the same kind as what comes before it, it enters into the ruling, otherwise not — and this is attributed to Abū al-ʿAbbās; and one says that if what comes after it is of a different kind from what comes before it, it does not enter, and if it is of the same kind, inclusion and non-inclusion are both possible. The first of these views is the most correct according to the grammarians. One of them said: that is because wherever we have found a contextual indicator with «إلى», that indicator requires exclusion from what precedes it; so when speech comes free of indicators, it should be taken according to the common and frequent case, which is exclusion. This speaker distinguished between «إلى» and «حتى», making «حتى» require inclusion and «إلى» require exclusion by the evidence mentioned. The proofs of these views are found elsewhere than in this book, and I have explained them in my book "Sharḥ al-Tashīl". The second view: that it is in the sense of «مع», i.e. "together with the elbows"; the discussion of this has preceded at His saying: {إلى أَمْوَالِكُمْ} [al-Nisāʾ: 2]. «المرافق» is the plural of «مَرْفِق», with fatḥa on the mīm and kasra on the fāʾ in the most eloquent usage; it is the joint between the upper arm and the forearm.

His saying: {بِرُؤُوسِكُمْ}: there are three views on this bāʾ. One of them: that it is for adhesion (ilṣāq), i.e. "make the wiping adhere to your heads". Al-Zamakhsharī said: "What is meant is the adhesion of the wiping to the head; one who wipes part of it and one who covers it entirely with wiping both make the wiping adhere to his head." The Shaykh [Abū Ḥayyān] said: "It is not as he mentioned," meaning that one who wipes part of his head is not described as making the wiping adhere to his head. This is a quibble of no value. The second: that it is redundant (zāʾida), like His saying: {وَلاَ تُلْقُواْ بِأَيْدِيكُمْ} [al-Baqara: 195], and the poet's saying:

169 - 9-. . . . . . . . . . . ... . . . . . . . . . لا يَقْرَأْنَ بالسُّوَرِ
(… they do not recite the sūras)

This is the apparent sense of Sībawayh's words, for he related «خَشَّنْتُ صدرَه وبصدره» ("I roused his breast to anger") and «مَسَحْتُ رأسَه وبرأسِه» ("I wiped his head") with one meaning. Al-Farrāʾ said: "The Arabs say: «خُذِ الخِطامَ وبالخطام» ('take the halter'), «هَزَّه وهَزَّ به» ('he shook it') and «خُذْ برأسِه ورأسَه» ('take him by the head')." The third: that it is partitive (li-l-tabʿīḍ), like the poet's saying:

170 - 0- شَرِبْنَ بماءِ البحرِ ثم ترفَّعَتْ ... . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
(They drank of the sea's water, then rose up …)

This is a weak view; the discussion of this has preceded at the beginning of the basmala.

His saying: {وَأَرْجُلَكُمْ}: Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir, al-Kisāʾī and Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim read «أرجلَكم» in the accusative; the rest of the Seven read «وأرجلِكم» in the genitive; and al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan read «وأرجلُكم» in the nominative. As for the accusative reading, it has two explanations. One of them: that it is conjoined to «أيديكم», for its ruling is washing like the faces and the hands, as though it were said: "and wash your feet". However, some have invalidated this explanation on the ground that it entails separating the two conjoined elements by a clause that is not parenthetical, since that clause institutes a new ruling and so contains no emphasis of the first. Ibn ʿUṣfūr said — having mentioned separation between two conjoined elements —: "The ugliest it can be is with clauses", and his words show that it is not permissible to explain the verse thus. Abū al-Baqāʾ said the opposite of this, for he said: "It is conjoined to the faces", then said: "and that is permissible in Arabic without disagreement", and he made the Sunna that has come concerning washing the feet a support for this explanation. This is nothing, for someone may say: it is possible that the accusative is by conjunction with the position of the genitive noun, and its ruling was wiping, but that was abrogated by the Sunna — and this is a well-known view of the scholars. The second: that it is accusative by conjunction with the position of the genitive noun before it, as has been established before.

As for the genitive reading, it has four explanations. One of them: that it is accusative in meaning, conjoined to the hands that are washed, and is made genitive only by proximity (ʿalā al-jiwār), like their saying «هذا جُحْرُ ضبٍّ خَرِبٍ» ("this is a ruined lizard's hole") with «خرب» in the genitive, although its due was the nominative, since in meaning it is an adjective of the hole, because the hole can be described by it, whereas the lizard cannot; it was made genitive only by proximity. This issue has a condition according to the grammarians, namely that ambiguity be avoided, as in the example given — unlike «قام غلام زيد العاقل» ("Zayd's intelligent servant stood"): if you make «العاقل» an adjective of the servant, making it genitive by proximity is impossible because of the ambiguity. He also cited the poet's saying:

170 - 1- كأنما ضَرَبَتْ قُدَّامَ أعينِها ... قُطْناً بمستحصِدِ الأوتارِ مَحْلوجِ
(As though she had struck before her eyes, with a taut-stringed bow, carded cotton)

And another's saying:

170 - 2- فأياكم وَحيَّةَ بَطْنِ وادٍ ... هموزٍ النابِ ليس لكم بِسِيِّ
(Beware of a valley-bed serpent with a piercing fang; it is no equal of yours)

And another's saying:

170 - 3- كأن ثَبيراً في عرانينِ وَبْلِه ... كبيرُ أُناسٍ في بِجادٍ مُزَمَّلِ
(As though Thabīr, at the onset of its downpour, were a people's elder wrapped in a striped cloak)

And another's saying:

170 - 4- كأنَّ نَسْجَ العنكبوتِ المُرْمَل ...
(As though the woven spider's web …)

— with «محلوج» in the genitive although it is an adjective of the accusative «قطنا»; «هموز» in the genitive although it is an adjective of the accusative «حية»; «المزمل» in the genitive although it is an adjective of «كبير», since it means "wrapped up"; and «المُرْمل» in the genitive although it is an adjective of «نَسْج». These were made genitive only because of proximity. Al-Aʿmash read: {إنَّ الله هو الرزاقُ ذو القوةِ المتينِ} with «المتين» in the genitive by proximity to «القوة», although it is an adjective of «الرزاق». Although this does occur, explaining the verse by it is weak, because proximity is weak in general; moreover, genitive by proximity has come only in the naʿt (adjective), not in conjunction, and it has come rarely in tawkīd (emphasis) under poetic necessity; he said:

170 - 5- يا صاحِ بَلَّغ ذوي الزوجاتِ كلِّهمِ ... أَنْ ليسَ وَصْلٌ إذا انْحَل‍َّتْ عُرَى الذَّنَبِ
(O friend, tell all those who have wives that there is no union once the knots of the tail have come undone)

— with «كلهم» in the genitive although it is a tawkīd of the accusative «ذوي». If it has come only in the naʿt, or in what is anomalous apart from it, then the Book of Allah the Exalted should not be explained by it. I have explained this issue and mentioned its evidence in "Sharḥ al-Tashīl". Among those who stated explicitly that explaining the verse by proximity is weak is Makkī ibn Abī Ṭālib and others. Makkī said: "Al-Akhfash and Abū ʿUbayda said: 'The genitive in it is by proximity, and the meaning is washing.' This is far-fetched; the Qurʾān is not to be interpreted by it." Abū al-Baqāʾ said: "It is the i'rab of which it is said: it is by proximity. It is not impossible for it to occur in the Qurʾān, because it is frequent; it has come in the Qurʾān and in poetry. From the Qurʾān is His saying, Exalted is He: {وَحُورٌ عِينٌ} [al-Wāqiʿa: 22] in the reading of those who read it in the genitive, it being conjoined to His saying {بِأَكْوَابٍ وَأَبَارِيقَ} although it differs in meaning, since the meaning is not 'immortal youths will go round among them with wide-eyed houris'. And al-Nābigha said:

170 - 6- لم يَبْقَ إلاَّ أسيرٌ غيرُ مُنْفَلِتٍ ... أو مُوْثَقٍ في حبال القومِ مَجْنُوبِ
(None remained but a captive who could not escape, or one bound in the people's ropes, led alongside)

— the rhymes being genitive. Proximity is well known among them in i'rab." Then he mentioned many things that he claimed support his claim. Among them: the inversion of i'rab in adjectives, like His saying, Exalted is He: {عَذَابَ يَوْمٍ مُّحِيطٍ} [Hūd: 84], whereas the day is not encompassing — only the punishment encompasses; and similarly His saying, Exalted is He: {فِي يَوْمٍ عَاصِفٍ} [Ibrāhīm: 18], whereas «عاصف» is not a description of the day but of the wind. Among them: changing some letters into others, like his saying, upon him be peace: «ارجَعْنَ مَأْزوراتٍ غيرَ مأجورات» ("go back burdened with sin, not rewarded"), the original being «مَوْزورات», but correspondence of form was intended; and likewise their saying «إنه ليأتينا بالغدايا والعَشايا» ("he comes to us mornings and evenings"), meaning that the original is «بالغَدَاوى», since it is from «الغُدْوة», but because of the yāʾ of «العشايا» it came with yāʾ rather than wāw. Among them: treating a masculine as feminine, as in His saying, Exalted is He: {فَلَهُ عَشْرُ أَمْثَالِهَا} [al-Anʿām: 160], where He omitted the tāʾ from «عشر» although it is annexed to «الأمثال», which is masculine; but since «الأمثال» is adjacent to the feminine pronoun, He applied its ruling to it. Likewise the poet's saying:

170 - 7- لَمَّا أتى خبرُ الزبيرِ تواضعتْ ... سورُ المدينةِ والجبالُ الخُشَّعُ
(When the news of al-Zubayr came, the wall of Medina and the humbled mountains bowed low)

and their saying «ذَهَبَتْ بعضُ أصابعِه» ("some of his fingers went"), meaning that «سور» is masculine and «بعض» likewise, but since they are adjacent to a feminine they were given its ruling. Among them: «قامت هند» — when they do not separate they bring the tāʾ, and when they separate they do not bring it, and there is no difference except adjacency and its absence. Among them: their preferring the accusative in ishtighāl after a verbal clause, in their saying «قام زيدٌ وعمراً كلمته» ("Zayd stood, and ʿAmr I spoke to"), because of adjacency to the verb. Among them: their changing the wāw adjacent to the end of the word into a hamza, as in «أوائل», unlike «طواويس», because it is far from adjacency to the end. He said: "This is a place in which pages of evidence could be written. The grammarians have devoted a chapter to it, arranged issues upon it, and based it on their saying «هذا جُحْرُ ضبٍ خربٍ», to the point that they disagreed over whether the dual and plural may be made genitive; a group of their experts permitted following [by proximity] in both, by analogy with the singular that is heard. Had it no basis at all, they would have restricted it to what is heard only. What we have mentioned is supported by the fact that something other than the genitive has been permitted in the verse — namely the nominative and the accusative — and the nominative and accusative are neither decisive nor apparent in indicating that the ruling of the feet is wiping; so likewise the genitive must be like the accusative and nominative in the ruling, though not in the i'rab." End of quotation.

As for his saying that {وَحُورٌ عِينٌ} belongs to this category, it is nothing, because either one supposes them conjoined to what precedes — with an interpretation that people have mentioned, as will come, or without interpretation — or one does not conjoin them. If one conjoins them to what precedes, the genitive is necessary; if one does not conjoin them, the genitive is not permissible. As for their being genitive according to what people have mentioned, it was said: it is by their conjunction with the noun made genitive by the bāʾ before them, on the basis that the preceding verb implies "they take delight and enjoy themselves with cups and such-and-such"; or the verb is not made to imply anything, and the youths' going round with the wide-eyed houris among the people of Paradise is a delight to them. [Genitive by] proximity applies only where the noun deserves something other than the genitive and is made genitive because of adjacency to what precedes it; whereas this — as you see — he himself declared to be conjoined to «بأكواب». The most that can be said is that he made it differ in meaning, meaning that in his view it is not permissible to conjoin them to «بأكواب» except with another sense, namely the verb's implying [another meaning]; and this does not impair the conjunction. As for the verse, the genitive of «موثقٍ» is not because of its proximity to «منفلتٍ»; rather it is in consideration of the noun made genitive by «غير», because they have stated that if after «غير» and its genitive noun you bring a follower, it may follow the wording of «غير» or follow the muḍāf ilayhi; and they cited this verse. It is also narrated: «لم يبق فيها طريدٌ غيرُ منفلتٍ» ("there remained in it no fugitive who could not escape"). As for the remaining examples he brought, they are not of the proximity that affects a change of i'rab. It has preceded that the grammarians restricted this to the naʿt, and that it has come in tawkīd under poetic necessity.

The second explanation: that it is conjoined to «برؤوسكم» in wording and meaning, and then that was abrogated by the obligation of washing — or it is a ruling that still stands, which a group held — or the wiping of the feet is taken to refer to one of the states, namely wearing the leather sock (khuff); this is attributed to al-Shāfiʿī. The third explanation: that they were made genitive as a warning against extravagance in using water, since they are a place where water is likely to be poured abundantly; so they were conjoined to what is wiped, while what is meant is washing them, for the reason given. Al-Zamakhsharī took this view. He said: "And it was said: «إلى الكعبين» — the limit was brought to remove the notion of one who might think them to be wiped, since no limit has been set for wiping in the Sharīʿa." It is as though he was not satisfied with this view that repels this misconception, and it is as he said. The fourth explanation: that they are genitive by an implied preposition indicated by the meaning, this preposition being attached to a verb that is also omitted and suits the context; so the omission of a verbal clause and the omission of a preposition are claimed. They said: its implied form is «وافعَلُوا بأرجلِكم غسلاً» ("and do washing to your feet").

Abū al-Baqāʾ said: "Omitting the preposition and keeping the genitive is permissible, as in the poet's saying:

170 - 8- مشائيمُ ليسوا مُصْلِحينَ عشيرةً ... ولا ناعبٍ إلا بِبَيْنٍ غرابُها
(Ill-omened folk who set no clan right, and whose crow croaks only of parting)

And another said:

170 - 9- بدا ليَ أنِّي لستُ مُدْرِكَ ما مضى ... ولا سابقٍ شيئاً إذا كان جائِيا
(It became clear to me that I cannot overtake what has passed, nor outrun anything when it is coming)

— it is made genitive by implying the bāʾ, and it is not a place of poetic necessity. I have devoted a book to this issue." His saying "and keeping the genitive" is not to be taken absolutely; rather it is regular only in certain places that the authorities on the language have specified, and this is not one of them. As for the two verses, the genitive in them is called by the grammarians "conjunction by supposition" (al-ʿaṭf ʿalā al-tawahhum), meaning as though he supposed the presence of the bāʾ as redundant in the khabar of «ليس», since its addition there is frequent. They compared this to His saying, Exalted is He: {فَأَصَّدَّقَ وَأَكُن مِّنَ الصالحين} [al-Munāfiqūn: 10], with «أَكُنْ» in the jussive by conjunction with «فأصَّدَّق» on the supposition of the absence of the fāʾ from «فأصَّدَّق»; Sībawayh and others stated this explicitly. Thus the unsoundness of this explanation is evident.

As for the nominative reading, it is as a mubtadaʾ (subject) with the khabar (predicate) omitted, i.e. "and your feet are washed" or "wiped", according to what has preceded on their ruling. The discussion of His saying «إلى الكعبين» is like the discussion of «إلى المرفقين». [Translator's note: the source writes «المرفقين» here, while the verse has «المرافق».] On «الكعبان» there are two well-known views. The better known of them: that they are the two protruding bones at the joint of the shin and the foot — in each foot there are two ankles. The second: that it is the protruding bone on the top of the foot where the sandal-strap meets. What the verse means is the first. «الكعبة» is any square house; its explanation will come in its place.

His saying: «منه» is in the position of the accusative, attached to «امسحوا». On «مِنْ» in it there are two views. The more apparent of them: that it is partitive. The second: that it is for the beginning of the extent; for this reason, according to these people, it is not a condition that dust cling to the hand. His saying «ليجعلَ»: the discussion of this lām is like the discussion of it at His saying: {يُرِيدُ الله لِيُبَيِّنَ لَكُمْ} [al-Nisāʾ: 26]; except that whoever makes the object of the intending omitted and attaches to it the lām of «ليجعلَ» makes «مِنْ» redundant in an affirmative context in His saying «من حرج»; that was allowed because it is within the domain of negation, even though the negation does not fall on the verb of the "hardship". «من حرج» is the object of «ليجعل». The «جعل» may be in the sense of bringing into being and creating, so it is transitive to one object, namely «من حرج», «مِنْ» being redundant in it as has preceded; and «عليكم» is then attached to the «جعل». It may also be attached to «حرج». If it is said: it is a maṣdar, and a maṣdar's governed element does not precede it — it is said: that applies to the maṣdar interpreted as a maṣdar particle and a verb, because it is in the sense of a relative; and this is not interpreted as a maṣdar particle. The «جعل» may also be in the sense of making something become something (taṣyīr), so «عليكم» would be the second object.

His saying: {عَلَيْكُم}: there are three views on it. The most apparent of them: that it is attached to «يتم». The second: that it is attached to «نعمته». The third: that it is attached to an omitted element as a ḥāl from «نعمته». Abū al-Baqāʾ mentioned these last two views. This verse differs from the one before it in His saying: {وَأَتْمَمْتُ عَلَيْكُمْ نِعْمَتِي} [al-Māʾida: 3], where attaching the preposition and its noun to «النعمة» was impossible because the governed element of the maṣdar preceded it, as was explained. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "And it was read «فَأَطْهِروا», i.e. purify your bodies; and likewise «ليُطْهِركم»." He means that it was read «أَطْهِروا» as an imperative from the four-letter «أَطْهَر», like «أَكْرم». People attributed the second reading — I mean His saying «لِيُطْهِرَكم» — to Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib.

semin-durr:39-39.t: His saying, Exalted is He: {مِن بَعْدِ ظُلْمِهِ}: attached to «تاب». «ظلم» is a maṣdar (verbal noun) annexed to its agent, i.e. "after he wronged another by taking his property," and this is clear. Some allowed it to be annexed to the object, i.e. "after he wronged himself." The permissibility of this is open to question, since the implied form becomes "after he wronged him," and if this underlying form were stated explicitly it would not be permissible, because it leads to the verb of a pronoun passing over to its own attached pronoun, which is permitted only in the chapter of ظنّ, فَقَدَ and عَدِم. So said the Shaykh [Abū Ḥayyān]. His objection is itself open to question, because when we resolve the maṣdar into a maṣdar particle and a verb, we bring after the verb only what is valid to assume, namely the word «النفس», i.e. "after he wronged himself."

semin-durr:7-7.t: His saying, Exalted is He: {إِذْ قُلْتُمْ سَمِعْنَا}: there are three views on «إذا» [Translator's note: so in the source; the word in the verse is «إذ».]. The most apparent of them: that it is accusative (manṣūb) by «واثقكم». The second: that it is accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial) from the hāʾ in «به». The third: that it is a ḥāl from «ميثاقه». On these last two views it is attached to (mutaʿalliq) an omitted element, according to the established rule. «قلتم» is in the position of the genitive by the adverb, and «سَمِعْنا» is in the position of the accusative by the verb of saying.

semin-durr:8-8.t: His saying, Exalted is He: {كُونُواْ قَوَّامِينَ}: its parallel has preceded in al-Nisāʾ, except that there the word «القسط» was put first and here it is put later. It is as though the purpose of that — and Allah knows best — is that the verse of al-Nisāʾ came in the context of acknowledgement against oneself, one's parents and relatives, so it began with «القسط», which is justice without favouring oneself, a parent or a relative; whereas the one here came in the context of mentioning enmity, so it began with the command to stand for Allah, because that is a stronger deterrent for the believers, and then it followed with bearing witness in justice. So in each context what suits it was brought. His saying: {وَلاَ يَجْرِمَنَّكُم} [al-Māʾida: 2]: its like has preceded, and the appearance of the preposition here supports supposing it earlier. «هو أقرب»: «هو» is the pronoun of the maṣdar (verbal noun) understood from the verb, i.e. justice; it has many parallels that have preceded.

semin-durr:9-9.t: His saying, Exalted is He: {وَعَدَ الله}: «وعد» is transitive to two objects, the first of them being the relative noun and the second omitted, i.e. "Paradise"; this object is made explicit elsewhere than in this place. On this view the clause in His saying «لهم مغفرة» has no grammatical position, because it explains that omitted element in the way a cause explains its effect, for Paradise is the result of forgiveness and the attainment of the great reward; and the speech before it is complete in itself. Al-Zamakhsharī mentioned other possibilities in the verse. One of them: that the clause in His saying {لَهُم مَّغْفِرَةٌ} is an explanation of the promise, as though He said: He set forth a promise for them, and it was said: what did He promise? So He said: "For them is forgiveness and a great reward." On this view too it has no grammatical position; and this is better than the first, because explaining what is uttered is better than claiming the explanation of something omitted. The second: that the clause is accusative (manṣūb) by an omitted verb of saying, as though it were said: He promised them and said: "For them is forgiveness." The third: treating "promising" like "saying", since it is a kind of it, and making «وعد» fall on the clause that is His saying «لهم مغفرة», just as «تَرَكْنا» fell on His saying {سَلاَمٌ على نُوحٍ} [al-Ṣāffāt: 79], as though it were said: He promised them this saying; and when One Who does not break the promise has promised them, He has promised them its content of forgiveness and great reward. Treating promising like saying is a Kufan doctrine.

semin-durr:10-10.t: His saying, Exalted is He: {والذين كَفَرُواْ}: a mubtadaʾ (subject); «أولئك» is a second mubtadaʾ, «أصحاب» is its khabar (predicate), and the clause is the khabar of the first. This clause is resumptive (mustaʾnafa); it was brought as a nominal clause to indicate fixity and permanence, and it was not brought in the framework of the threat in the way the clause before it was brought in the framework of the promise, in order to cut off their hope. Some permitted this clause to fall within the domain of the promise, according to what was established for the clause before it. He said: "Because the threat that befalls their enemies is something that heals their breasts and removes the harm they used to suffer from them; and there is no doubt that harm befalling the enemy is something that gladdens and delights his enemy." This is open to consideration, for the resumption suffices for this meaning: when a person hears news that grieves his enemy he is gladdened by it, even if he was not promised it. The proponent of this aforementioned view may find support in the fact that al-Zamakhsharī inclined to this meaning in Sūrat Subḥān [al-Isrāʾ]; he said: "If you say: to what is {وأَنَّ الذين لاَ يُؤْمِنُونَ} [al-Isrāʾ: 10] conjoined? I say: to {أَنَّ لَهُمْ أَجْراً كَبِيراً} [al-Isrāʾ: 9], on the basis that He gave the believers two good tidings: of their reward and of the punishment of their enemies." So he made the punishment of their enemies fall within the domain of the good tidings; and the good tidings there are like the promise here.

semin-durr:11-11.t: His saying, Exalted is He: {عَلَيْكُمْ}: it may be attached to (mutaʿalliq) «نعمة», or attached to an omitted element as a ḥāl (circumstantial) from it. «إذ هم» is an adverb (ẓarf) whose governor is likewise «النعمة», i.e. remember His favour upon you at the time of their intending. This adverb may also be attached to what «عليكم» is attached to, if you make it a ḥāl from «نعمة». It is not permissible for it to be accusative by «اذكروا», because their times are incompatible, for «إذ» is for the past and «اذكروا» is future. «أن يَبْسُطوا» is on the dropping of the bāʾ, i.e. "they intended to stretch out"; so concerning the position of «أَنْ» there is the well-known disagreement.

semin-durr:12-12.t:
His saying, Exalted is He: {مِنهُمُ اثني عَشَرَ نَقِيباً}: «منهم» may be attached to (mutaʿalliq) «بَعَثْنا», or attached to an omitted element as a ḥāl (circumstantial) from «اثني عشر», because it was originally an adjective of it, and when it was put before it, it became accusative as a ḥāl. The discussion of the composition of «اثني عشر», its being indeclinable (mabnī) and the omission of its nūn has preceded in al-Baqara, which makes repeating it unnecessary. «ميثاق» may be annexed to its object — which is the apparent view — i.e. Allah the Exalted made a covenant with them; or annexed to its agent, i.e. they made a covenant with Him, Exalted is He. In the mufāʿala form the act may be attributed to each of the two mentioned parties. «النقيب» is of the pattern faʿīl. It was said: in the sense of an active participle (fāʿil), derived from «النَّقْب», which is searching out; of this is {فَنَقَّبُواْ فِي البلاد} [Qāf: 36]. He was so called because he searches out the conditions and secrets of the people. It was also said: it is in the sense of a passive participle (mafʿūl), as though the people chose him with knowledge from searching out his conditions. It was also said: it is for intensiveness, like «عليم» and «خبير».

His saying: {لَئِنْ أَقَمْتُمُ}: this lām is the lām that prepares for the oath (al-mūṭṭiʾa li-l-qasam), and the oath with it is omitted. It has preceded that when a condition and an oath come together, the first of them is answered, unless something having a khabar precedes, in which case the condition is answered absolutely. His saying: {لأُكَفِّرَنَّ}: this lām is the answer of the oath because it came first, and the apodosis (jawāb al-sharṭ) is omitted because the answer of the oath indicates it. This is the meaning of al-Zamakhsharī's saying that His saying «لأكفرنَّ» stands in place of the answers of both the oath and the condition — not as some understood it and then refuted him on that basis. «لأكفرن» may also be the answer to His saying, Exalted is He, before that: {وَلَقَدْ أَخَذَ الله مِيثَاقَ بني إِسْرَآئِيلَ}, because the covenant implies the meaning of an oath. On this view the two clauses — I mean His saying «وبعثنا» and «وقال الله» — admit two views. One of them: that they are in the position of the accusative as a ḥāl. The second: that they are two parenthetical clauses. The apparent view is that the answer of His saying {لَئِنْ أَقَمْتُمُ} is «لأكفرنَّ», as has preceded, and that the whole of this conditioned oath and its answer is explicative of that aforementioned covenant.

«التعزير» is honouring; he said:

171 - 0- وكم من ماجدٍ لهُمُ كريمٍ ... ومِنْ لَيْثٍ يُعَزَّرُ في النَّدِيِّ
(How many a glorious, noble man they have, and how many a lion honoured in the assembly)

It was also said: it is praising with good — Yūnus said this — and it is close to the first. It was also said: it is repelling from wrongdoing — al-Farrāʾ said this. Al-Zajjāj said: "It is deterring and preventing." On the first two views the meaning is: "and you honoured them and praised them well"; and on the third and fourth the meaning is: "and you repelled and deterred their fools from them". Al-Zajjāj said: "«عزرت فلاناً» means: I did to him what deters him from what is ugly, like «نَكَّلت»; on this view «عَزَّرْتُموهم» means you repelled their enemies from them." Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī read «برسْلي» with sukūn on the ʿayn [i.e. the middle radical] wherever it occurs. Al-Jaḥdarī read «وعَزَرْتموهم» with the zāy without doubling, and it is a dialect form. In al-Fatḥ he read «وتَعْزُروه» with fatḥa on the imperfect prefix, sukūn on the ʿayn and ḍamma on the zāy, which agrees with his reading here. [Translator's note: the source prints «وتَعْزُوروه», apparently a misprint.]

His saying: {وَأَقْرَضْتُمُ الله قَرْضاً}: the discussion of «قَرْضا» and of its accusative case has preceded in al-Baqara.

semin-durr:96-96.t:
His saying, Exalted is He: {وَطَعَامُهُ}: conjoined (nasq) to «صيد», i.e. "lawful for you are the hunting and its food." So «الصيد» is the act of hunting, and «الطعام» is the act of feeding, i.e. it is an ism maṣdar (noun standing for the verbal noun); in that case the object is taken as omitted, i.e. "your feeding yourselves with it." And «الصيد» may be in the sense of «المَصِيد» (the game hunted). On this view the hāʾ in «طعامُه» refers back to the sea, i.e. "lawful for you are the game of the sea and the food of the sea," so on this view the food is something other than the game; there is a disagreement about it among the exegetes, which I mentioned in its place. On this view the hāʾ may also refer back to «الصيد» in the sense of the game hunted. And «طعام» may be in the sense of «مَطْعوم» (what is eaten); this is indicated by the reading of Ibn ʿAbbās and ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ḥārith: «وطَعْمُه» with ḍamma on the mīm and sukūn on the ʿayn.
[Translator's note: the source says "with ḍamma on the mīm and sukūn on the ʿayn"; the ḍamma on the mīm is the nominative ending of the word, the distinctive feature being the sukūn of the ʿayn.]

His saying: {مَتَاعاً}: there are two views on its being accusative (manṣūb). The first: it is accusative as a maṣdar (mafʿūl muṭlaq, absolute object); this is the view of Makkī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Abū al-Baqāʾ and others, the implied form being: "He has given you enjoyment of it as an enjoyment from which you benefit and which you take as a relish." Makkī said: "Because His saying «أُحِلَّ لكم» has the meaning 'I have given you enjoyment of it as an enjoyment,' like His saying {كِتَابَ الله عَلَيْكُمْ} [al-Nisāʾ: 24]."

The second: it is a mafʿūl li-ajlihi (object of purpose). Al-Zamakhsharī said: "That is: He made it lawful for you as a provision of enjoyment for you. In the case of the mafʿūl lahu it occupies the same place as His saying, Exalted is He, {وَوَهَبْنَا لَهُ إِسْحَاقَ وَيَعْقُوبَ نَافِلَةً} [al-Anbiyāʾ: 72] in the chapter of the ḥāl (circumstantial); for His saying {مَتَاعاً لَّكُمْ} is a mafʿūl lahu specific to the food, just as «نافلةً» is a ḥāl specific to Yaʿqūb. He means: its food has been made lawful for you as a provision of enjoyment for those of you who stay, who eat it fresh, and for your travellers, who take it as provision dried." End of quotation.

So al-Zamakhsharī made its being a mafʿūl lahu specific to the verb — namely «أُحِلَّ» — as attributed to His saying {وَطَعَامُهُ}; it is not a reason for the lawfulness of the game, but a reason for the lawfulness of the food only. What led him to that is his school — which is the school of Abū Ḥanīfa — that the game of the sea is divided into what is eaten and what is not eaten, and that its food is what is eaten from it, and that the provision of enjoyment applies only to what is eaten of it, fresh or dried. [Translator's note: the source has «لا يقع التمثيل» ("the illustration does not apply"), apparently a copyist's slip for «التمتيع» ("the provision of enjoyment"); it is rendered by the latter sense.] And his saying «نافلةً» means that this ḥāl is specific to Yaʿqūb, because he is a grandson, unlike Isḥāq, who is his son of his own loins, and «النافلة» is applied only to a grandchild, not to a child; and likewise «متاعاً».

However, this leads to a single verb being attributed to two conjoined agents, being given a reason in its attribution to one of them and not so in the other. If you say «قام زيد وعمرو إجلالاً لك» ("Zayd and ʿAmr stood out of reverence for you"), it would then be possible that Zayd's standing is the one specific to reverence, or the reverse, and this involves ambiguity. As for the ḥāl that he cited in the noble verse, there is a contextual indicator there which required the ḥāl to be referred to one of the two, unlike the noble verse we are dealing with. As for [those of] other than his school, for them it is a mafʿūl lahu not specific to either of the two conjoined terms, and that is plain and clear.

And «لكم»: if we say that «متاعاً» is a maṣdar, it may be a naʿt (adjective) of it, and it is then a maṣdar specifying [the type], because it has been qualified. If we say that it is a mafʿūl lahu, then it is attached to an omitted verb, i.e. "I mean: for you," as in «قمتُ إجلالاً لك» ("I stood out of reverence for you"). And the lām may be a strengthening lām for the transitivity of the maṣdar, since the implied form is "so that I give you enjoyment" and "so that I revere you"; and so too with its parallels.

His saying: {مَا دُمْتُمْ}: «ما» is maṣdariyya (verbal-noun-forming), and «دمتم» is its ṣila (relative clause); it is a maṣdariyya ẓarfiyya (temporal verbal-noun particle), i.e. "the game of the land has been forbidden to you for the duration of your continuing in iḥrām." The majority read the dāl of «دمتم» with ḍamma, from the dialect of those who say «دام يدوم». Yaḥyā read {دِمتم} with kasra, from the dialect of those who say «دام يدام», like «خاف يخاف»; the two are like the two dialects in «مات يموتُ» and «يَمات», as was stated earlier.

The majority read «وحُرِّم» in the passive, with «صيدُ» nominative as standing in place of the fāʿil (agent). And it has been read «وحَرَّم» in the active, with «صيدَ» accusative as the mafʿūl bihi (direct object).

The majority also read «حُرُماً» with ḍamma on the ḥāʾ and the rāʾ, the plural of «حَرام» in the sense of «مُحْرِم» (one in iḥrām), like «قَذال» and «قُذُل». Ibn ʿAbbās read {حَرَماً} with fatḥa on both, i.e. "possessors of ḥaram," i.e. of iḥrām. It has been said: He made them like the place that is barred. The best is that it be of the type «رجل عدل» ("a man [who is] justice"): He made them the very maṣdar, for «حَرَما» is in the sense of «إحرام»; and it was stated earlier that the maṣdar applies to one and to more with a single form.

And «البَرّ» (land) is well known. Al-Layth said: "It is used as an indefinite; one says: «جلست بَرَّا» ('I sat outdoors') and «خرجْتُ براً» ('I went out to open country')." Al-Azharī said: "That is from the speech of the muwalladūn (post-classical speakers)." But this is open to question, given the saying of Salmān al-Fārisī: "Every man has a «جَوَّانِيّ» and a «بَرَّانِيّ»," i.e. an inner and an outer, and that is an alteration of the nisba (relative adjective) form. A full treatment of this root was given earlier in al-Baqara.

And He placed «إليه» before «تُحْشرون» for restriction, i.e. "you will be gathered to Him and not to another," or for the harmony of the verse-endings.

semin-durr:97-97.t:
His saying, Exalted is He: {جَعَلَ الله}: there are two views on it. The first: it is in the sense of «صَيَّر» (to make into), so it is transitive to two objects, the first of them «الكعبة» and the second «قياماً». The second: it is in the sense of «خلق» (to create), so it is transitive to one object, namely «الكعبة», and «قياماً» is accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial). Some said that «جعل» here is in the sense of «بَيَّن» (to make clear) and «حَكَم» (to decree); this ought to be taken as an explanation of the meaning, not as an explanation of the language, since the experts in Arabic have not transmitted that it occurs in the sense of «بَيَّن» or «حَكَم»; but making-clear is a necessary consequence of «الجَعْل».

As for «البيتَ», its being accusative is on one of two views: either as a badal (substitute) or as ʿaṭf bayān (explicative apposition). The benefit of that is that some of the people of the Jāhiliyya — namely Khathʿam — named a house "the Yemeni Kaʿba," so this badal or bayān was brought to distinguish it from anything else. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "«البيتَ الحرامَ» is ʿaṭf bayān by way of praise, not by way of clarification, just as the naʿt (adjective) comes in that way." The Shaykh [Abū Ḥayyān] objected to him that the condition of the bayān is that it be a non-derived (jāmid) noun, and a non-derived noun does not convey praise; only a derived noun conveys it. Then he said: "Unless he means that, since «البيت» was qualified by «الحرام», the combination requires that, in which case it is possible."

And «الكعبة» linguistically is any square house, and the Kaʿba was called Kaʿba for that reason. The root of its derivation is «الكَعْب», which is one of the members of the human body. Al-Rāghib said: "«كَعْبُ الرجل» is [the bone] that is at the meeting of the shank and the foot; «الكعبة» is any house in its shape in squareness, and after it the Kaʿba was named. And Dhū al-Kaʿabāt was a house belonging to Banū Rabīʿa in the Jāhiliyya. And «امرأة كاعِب» is a woman whose breasts have become rounded (تكعَّب)." Discussion of this root was given earlier at the beginning of the sūra.

The majority read here «قياماً» with an alif after the yāʾ, and Ibn ʿĀmir «قِيَماً» without an alif, on the pattern of «عِنَب». «القيام» here may be a maṣdar (verbal noun) of «قام - يقوم», the meaning being that Allah made the Kaʿba a cause for people's rising toward it, i.e. for visiting it and making pilgrimage to it; or because the affair of their religion and their worldly life is set right at it, and by it they are sustained (يقومون). And «القيام» may be in the sense of «القِوام» (support, mainstay), the wāw having been changed into yāʾ because of the kasra before it; so said al-Wāḥidī. But this is open to question, since there is nothing that requires its weakening, as it is like «السِّواك»; rather it should be said that «القِيام» and «القِوام» have one meaning. [The poet] said:
181 - 2- قِوامُ دنيا وقِوامُ دينِ
(A mainstay of worldly life and a mainstay of religion.)
But when the tāʾ of femininity enters it, the yāʾ is obligatory, as in «القيامة».

As for the reading of Ibn ʿĀmir, some found it problematic, on the grounds that it must be one of two things: either a maṣdar on the pattern «فِعَل», or on the pattern «فِعال». If it is the first, the wāw ought to remain sound, as in «حِوَل» and «عَوَر»; and if it is the second, shortening occurs only in poetry. [Translator's note: «عَوَر» is on the pattern «فَعَل», not «فِعَل»; it is cited as written.]

Al-Jaḥdarī read «قَيِّماً» with a doubled yāʾ; it is a noun indicating the permanence of the quality. Its verification was given earlier at the beginning of al-Nisāʾ.

His saying: {والشهر الحرام والهدي والقلائد}: conjoined to «الكعبة», and the second object, or the ḥāl, is omitted because the meaning is understood, i.e. "Allah also made the month, the offering and the garlands a mainstay (قياماً)."

And «ذلك» admits three views. The first: it is the khabar (predicate) of an omitted mubtadaʾ (subject), i.e. "the ruling that We have decreed is that, and not something else." The second: it is a mubtadaʾ whose khabar is omitted, i.e. "that ruling is the truth, and not something else." The third: it is accusative by an implied (muqaddar) verb indicated by the context, i.e. "Allah has legislated that"; and this is the strongest of them, because the lām of cause is attached to it.

And «تعلموا» is accusative by an implied «أَنْ» after the lām of kay, not by the lām itself. And «أَنَّ الله» together with what falls within its scope stands in the place of the two objects, or of one of them, according to the disagreement mentioned earlier. And {وَأَنَّ الله بِكُلِّ شَيْءٍ عَلِيمٌ} is conjoined to the «أنَّ» before it.

semin-durr:41-41.t:
His saying, Exalted is He: {لاَ يَحْزُنكَ الذين}: it was stated earlier that «يحزن» is read with a fatḥa on the yāʾ and with a ḍamma on it, that the two are dialectal variants, and [it was discussed] whether they have one meaning or there is a difference between them. The prohibition is apparently addressed to «الذين», and it is of the type of the saying «لا أُرَيَنَّكَ ههنا» (let me not see you here), i.e. do not engage in causes through which sorrow comes to you on their account; the full treatment of this has been given to you several times. Abū al-Baqāʾ's statement on «يحزنك»: "The good [reading] is with a fatḥa on the yāʾ and a ḍamma on the zāy; it is also read with a ḍamma on the yāʾ and a kasra on the zāy, from «أحزنني», and it is a dialectal variant" — is not good, because it is a mass-transmitted (mutawātir) reading; its proof was given in Āl ʿImrān. «يُسارعون» is from «المسارعة» (hastening), and «في الكفر» is attached to the verb before it; its parallel was given in Āl ʿImrān.

His saying: {مِنَ الذين قالوا}: it may be a ḥāl (circumstantial) from the agent in «يُسارعون», i.e. they hasten while being some of those who said; it may be a ḥāl from the relative itself, which is close in meaning to the first; and «مِنْ» may be explaining the genus of the first relative, and likewise the second «مِنْ», so that it is an explanation and division of those who hasten into disbelief; on this view «سَمَّاعون» is the khabar (predicate) of an omitted mubtadaʾ (subject). «آمنَّا» is in the accusative by «قالوا», and «بأفواههم» is attached to «قالوا», not to «آمنَّا», in the sense that their saying did not go beyond their mouths: they only uttered it without believing it in their hearts. His saying {وَلَمْ تُؤْمِن قُلُوبُهُمْ} is a circumstantial (ḥāl) clause.

His saying: {وَمِنَ الذين هِادُواْ}: there are two views on it. First: what was stated above, namely that it is conjoined to «من الذين قالوا», as explanation and division. Second: that it is a fronted khabar and «سَمَّاعون» is a mubtadaʾ, the implied form being "and among those who are Jews are a people who listen much," so it is a resumptive sentence. However, the first view is given preference by the reading of al-Ḍaḥḥāk: «سَمَّاعين», in the accusative of censure by an omitted verb; this shows that the speech is not an independent sentence, but that His saying {وَمِنَ الذين هِادُواْ} is conjoined to «من الذين قالوا».

His saying «سَمَّاعون» is an intensive form. On «للكذب» there are two views. First: the lām is redundant (zāʾida) and «الكذب» is the object, i.e. "listening much to lies." The addition of the lām here is regular because the governor is a derived [i.e. non-verbal] one, so it is strengthened by the lām; similar is {فَعَّالٌ لِّمَا يُرِيدُ} [Hūd: 107].
