Then, if it denotes non-rational beings, it is put into the diminutive and pluralized with alif and tāʾ, so you say in the diminutive of «حُمُر», the plural of «حمار»: «حُمَيْرات»; and if it denotes rational beings, it is put into the diminutive and pluralized with wāw and nūn, so you say in the diminutive of «رجال»: «رُجَيْلون». And if it is an ism jamʿ (collective noun) like «قوم» and «رهط», or an ism jins (generic noun) like «قمر» and «شجر», it is put into the diminutive on its own form like all other singulars.

Returning to «أشياء»: their forming its diminutive on its own form indicates that it is an ism jamʿ, because the ism jamʿ is put into the diminutive on its own form, as in «رُهَيْط» and «قُوَيْم»; and it is not a broken plural, since it would be one of the plurals of multitude and it was not returned to its singular. This binds al-Akhfash because he is a Basran, and a Basran must do that; and «أُصَيْلان» is anomalous with him, so no analogy is drawn from it. In Makkī's wording he said: "Moreover, it binds them to form the diminutive of «أشياء» as «شُوَيَّات» or as «شُيَيْئات», and no one has said that." I say: his saying «شُوَيَّات» is not good, for this is not a place for changing yāʾ into wāw; do you not see that when you form the diminutive of «بيت» you say «بُيَيْت», not «بُوَيْت»? Except that the Kufans permit that, so he may hold their view.

Makkī also rejected the school of al-Farrāʾ and al-Akhfash by two things. The first: it entails the absence of a parallel, since «أَفْعِلاء» has not occurred as the plural of «فَيْعِل» such that this would be its parallel; and «هَيّن» with «أهْوناء» is anomalous, and no analogy is drawn from it. The second: that its deletion and weakening are carried out not according to rule. "So this view goes outside both analogy and transmitted usage in its pluralization and its weakening."

The fourth school — the view of al-Kisāʾī and Abū Ḥātim —: it is the plural of «شيء» on «أَفْعال», like «بَيْت» and «أبيات», and «ضيف» and «أضياف». People objected to this view that it entails diptote status without its cause, since if it were on «أَفْعال» it would be fully declinable like «أبيات». Al-Zajjāj said: "The Basrans and most of the Kufans agreed that al-Kisāʾī's view is wrong, and they bound him to make «أنباء» and «أسماء» diptotes." I say: al-Kisāʾī sensed this rebuttal and excused himself from it, but with what is not acceptable. Al-Kisāʾī, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "It — i.e. «أَشْياء» — is on the pattern «أَفْعال», but it became frequent in speech and so resembled «فَعْلاء», and was made a diptote just as «حَمْراء» is a diptote." He said: "And they pluralized it as «أَشاوَى», just as they pluralized «عَذْراء» as «عذارى» and «صَحْراء» as «صحارى»; and as «أَشْياوات», just as «حَمْراوات» is said." He means that they treated «أَشْياء», although it is on «أفعال», in the manner of «حَمْراء» and «عَذْراء» in both the broken and the sound plurals.

However, al-Farrāʾ and al-Zajjāj objected to this excuse. Al-Farrāʾ said: "If it were as he said, the more fitting of the two options would be that it be declined (tujrā), because when a word becomes frequent in speech it becomes light and may be declined, just as naming with «يزيد» became frequent and they declined it when indefinite, though it has an augment yāʾ that prevents declension." I say: by «الإجراء» he means full declension (al-ṣarf). And al-Zajjāj said: "The Basrans and most of the Kufans agreed…", which was given just above. Makkī said: "Al-Kisāʾī and Abū ʿUbayd said: it — i.e. «أشياء» — is a diptote because it resembled «حمراء», since the Arabs say «أَشْياوات» just as they say «حَمْراوات»." He said: "And it binds them both not to decline, in the plural, «أسماء» and «أبناء», given the Arabs' saying of them: «أسماوات» and «أبناوات»." I say: the explanation of this has been given. Then Makkī, after mentioning from al-Kisāʾī what I have given, and transmitting the school of al-Akhfash and al-Farrāʾ, said: "Abū Ḥātim said: «أَشْياء» is «أَفْعال», the plural of «شيء», like «أبيات»." This gives the impression that the school of al-Kisāʾī given earlier is other than this school; but it is not so — rather it is the very same.

I say: some answered on behalf of al-Kisāʾī that the grammarians, in the chapter of diptotes, took into account formal resemblance rather than resemblance in meaning. This is indicated by the question of «سراويل» in the dialect of those who make it a diptote, for there are two interpretations of it, one of them being that it is a foreign singular treated like its counterpart in pattern in Arabic, i.e. the form «مصابيح», for example. It is also indicated by their treating the shortened alif of ilḥāq (assimilation to a pattern) like the shortened alif of femininity, but together with proper-name status; so they took into account mere outward form. Were it not for fear of prolixity, I would mention many parallels to it.

The fifth school: its pattern is also «أَفْعِلاء», as the plural of «شَيِيء» on the pattern of «ظريف»; and «فَعيل» is pluralized on «أَفعلاء», like «نَصيب» and «أنْصِباء», and «صَدِيق» and «أَصْدقاء». Then the first hamza, which is the lām of the word, was deleted, and the yāʾ was given fatḥa so that the alif of the plural would remain sound, so it became «أَشْياء», and its pattern after the deletion is «أَفْعاء». Makkī made it, in morphology, like the morphological analysis of the school of al-Akhfash, inasmuch as the hamza is changed into a yāʾ and then one of the two yāʾs is deleted. He said, may Allah have mercy on him: "The deletion in the plural was made acceptable by its deletion in the singular; and it was deleted from the singular only for lightness, because of frequency of use, since «شيء» applies to every named thing, whether accident, substance or body; so it was made a diptote in the plural because of the hamza of femininity." [Translator's note: the source reads «فلم ينصرف همزةِ التأنيث», evidently missing «لـ» ("because of"); rendered by the evident sense.] He said: "And this is a good view, consistent in the plural, and its being a diptote is according to rule — were it not that the diminutive objects to it, as it objected to al-Akhfash." I say: his saying "this is a good view" is open to question, because of the many objections raised against it, which is evident from what has preceded.

When the Shaykh [Abū Ḥayyān] mentioned this school, he said in its morphological analysis: "Then the first hamza was deleted and the yāʾ of prolongation was given fatḥa because what follows it is an alif." He said: "Its pattern on this view became «أفياء», and on the view before it «أَفْلاء»." So I saw it written «أفياء» with a yāʾ, and this is a gross mistake; then I allowed that this may be a mistake made against him by the copyist, and that it was originally «أَفْعاء» with ʿayn, which the copyist misspelled as «أَفْياء». [Translator's note: the quoted words «ألى أفياء» and «إلا أَفْلاء» in the source evidently stand for «إلى أفياء» and «إلى أَفْلاء» ("became …"); rendered accordingly.]

People rejected this view on the grounds that [the claim] that the original of «شيء» is «شَيِيء» on the pattern of «صديق» is a claim without proof, and that [on it] it ought not to be put into the diminutive on its own form but returned to its singular, as was set out above.

The upshot of the discussion of «أشياء»: is it an ism jamʿ, whose original is «شَيْئاء» like «طَرْفاء», then its lām was transposed before its fāʾ so that its pattern became «لَفْعاء»; or is it an explicit plural? And if it is said to be an explicit plural, is its original «أَفْعِلاء», which then undergoes deletion and becomes «أَفْعاء» or «أَفْلاء»; or is its pattern «أفعال» like «أبيات»? Were it not for fear of departing from the purpose, I would have mentioned the question with all its aspects in full; but in this there is a sufficiency befitting this place.

His saying, Exalted is He: {إِن تُبْدَ}: a condition, and its apodosis (jawāb al-sharṭ) is «تَسُؤكم». This conditional clause is in the position of a genitive as a naʿt (adjective) of «أشياء», and likewise the conjoined conditional clause too. Ibn ʿAbbās read «إن تَبْدُ لكم تَسُؤْكم» with both verbs in the active, the imperfect prefix being tāʾ, with the fāʿil (agent) being the pronoun of «أشياء». Al-Shaʿbī read — according to what Abū Muḥammad ibn ʿAṭiyya transmitted from him — {إنْ يَبْدُ} with fatḥa on the yāʾ and ḍamma on the dāl, and «يَسُؤْكم» with fatḥa on the yāʾ, the fāʿil being a pronoun referring back to whatever is fitting to supply according to the meaning, i.e. "if your asking, or what you ask for, appears to you, it will grieve you." It cannot refer back to «أشياء», because that is treated as a metaphorical feminine, and whenever a verb is attributed to a feminine pronoun of any kind, the attachment of the [feminine] marker is obligatory on the correct view, and no attention is paid to poetic necessity. Others transmitted from al-Shaʿbī that he read {يُبْدَ لكم يَسُؤْكم} with yāʾ in both, except that he gave ḍamma to the first yāʾ and fatḥa to the second; the meaning being: "if the asking about them is made manifest (يُبْدَ), i.e. appears, that asking will grieve you," i.e. its answer, or the asking itself, because it is a cause of that; and the one who makes manifest is Allah the Exalted.

The pronoun in «عنها» may refer back to the kind of things that were forbidden, not to those very things; Ibn ʿAṭiyya said this, and al-Wāḥidī transmitted it from the author of "al-Naẓm", who gave as a parallel His saying, Exalted is He: {وَلَقَدْ خَلَقْنَا الإنسان مِن سُلاَلَةٍ مِّن طِينٍ} [al-Muʾminūn: 12], meaning Ādam, "then We made him" — he said: meaning the son of Ādam; so the pronoun referred back to what the first indicated. And it may refer back to those very things; al-Zamakhsharī said something to that effect.

His saying: {حِينَ يُنَزَّلُ القرآن}: there are two possibilities for this adverb. The first — which is the apparent one, and al-Zamakhsharī said nothing else —: it is accusative by «تسألوا». Al-Zamakhsharī said: "'And if you ask about them' — about these hard obligations — 'when the Quran is being sent down' — in the time of revelation, which is as long as the Messenger is among you receiving revelation — 'they will be shown to you,' those obligations which grieve you and which you are commanded to bear, and so you expose yourselves to Allah's anger through your neglect of them." From here I said to you that the pronoun in «عنها» refers back to the first «أشياء», not to their kind. The second: the adverb is accusative by «تُبْدَ لكم», i.e. "those things will appear to you at the time of the Quran's descent."

Some said: "There is fronting and postponement in the speech, because the implied order is: about things which, if you ask about them, will be shown to you at the time of the Quran's descent, and if they are shown to you, will grieve you." There is no doubt that the meaning is according to this order; except that this is not to be called fronting and postponement, for the wāw does not entail sequence, so there is no difference. Rather, this was only placed first before His saying {وَإِن تَسْأَلُواْ} for a benefit, namely deterrence from asking: He first told them that their asking about things which, whenever they appear, would grieve them, before informing them that if they asked about them they would be shown to them, so that they would be deterred; and that is a fitting meaning.

His saying: {عَفَا الله عَنْهَا}: there are two views on it. The first: it is in the position of a genitive, because it is another naʿt of «أشياء»; on this view the pronoun in «عنها» refers back to «أشياء». There is no need to claim fronting and postponement here, as some did, who said: "Its implied form is: do not ask about things which Allah has pardoned, which if they are shown to you… to the end of the verse"; for each of the two conditional clauses, and this clause, is a naʿt of «أشياء», so from where [does it follow] that this clause deserves to be placed before what precedes it? It is as though this speaker only supposed it to be fronted in order to make clear that it is a naʿt and not resumptive. The second: it has no grammatical position, because it is resumptive; on this view the pronoun in «عنها» refers back to the question indicated by «لا تَسْألوا», and it may refer back to «أشياء» — whereas on the first view this is required, by the necessity of a link between the naʿt and what it qualifies.

semin-durr:1-1.t:
This sūra is Medinan. In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. The parallel of His saying, Exalted is He: [verse 1] {يَا أَيُّهَا الذين آمَنُواْ أَوْفُواْ} has preceded. «البهيمة» is every four-legged creature on land or sea; and it is said «[Translator's note: the text has «وقل», apparently for «وقيل».]»: it is what is "obscure" (abhama) in respect of lacking speech and understanding. Everything on the pattern faʿīl or faʿīla whose middle radical is guttural may take kasra on its first radical, in harmony with its middle radical, as in «بيهمة» «[Translator's note: so in the text, apparently for «بهيمة».]», «شعيرة», «صغيرة» and «بحيرة». «الأنعام» — its explanation preceded in Āl ʿImrān.

His saying: {إِلاَّ مَا يتلى}: this is excepted from «بهيمة الأنعام», and the meaning is: what is recited to you as forbidden, namely His saying {حُرِّمَتْ عَلَيْكُمُ الميتة} [al-Māʾida: 3] up to His saying {وَمَا ذُبِحَ عَلَى النصب} [al-Māʾida: 3]. [There are two views on it. The first: that it is a connected exception (muttaṣil). The second:] that it is disconnected (munqaṭiʿ) — according to how what is recited to them is interpreted, as its explanation will come. On the supposition of its being a connected exception, its position admits two analyses. The more apparent: that it is accusative, because it is a connected exception from an affirmative statement. It may also be nominative as a naʿt (adjective) of «بهيمة», according to what is established in the science of grammar.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya transmitted from the Kufans two further analyses. The first: that it may be nominative as a badal (substitute) from «بهيمة». The second: that «إلا» is a conjunction and what follows it is conjoined to what precedes it. Then he said: "That is not permissible according to the Basrans except from an indefinite noun, or what approximates it among generic nouns, as in «جاء الرجالُ إلا زيدٌ» ('The men came, except Zayd'), as though you said: 'other than Zayd'." His saying "that" apparently refers to the two nominative analyses, the badal and the conjunction. His saying "except from an indefinite" is not apparent, because the badal is not permissible at all from an affirmative statement according to anyone among the Kufans and the Basrans; and agreement in definiteness and indefiniteness is not a condition in the badal. As for the conjunction, some of the Kufans mentioned it. As for what the Basrans made conditional on indefiniteness or what approximates it, they made it a condition only for qualification by «إلا» (al-naʿt bi-illā). So it is possible that the condition for the adjective became confused for Abū Muḥammad [Ibn ʿAṭiyya], and he made it a condition for the badal.

All this is if by what is recited to them as forbidden is meant His saying, Exalted is He: {حُرِّمَتْ عَلَيْكُمُ الميتة} [al-Māʾida: 3] to the end. If by it are meant the cattle, the gazelles, the wild cows and the wild asses, it is disconnected, in the sense of «لكن» according to the Basrans and in the sense of «بل» according to the Kufans. The explanation of this disconnected exception will come more fully than this shortly, when we treat the accusative of «غير».

His saying, Exalted is He: «غيرَ»: there are five analyses of its accusative. The first: that it is a ḥāl (circumstantial) from the genitive pronoun in «لكم»; this is the view of the majority, and al-Zamakhsharī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya and others adopted it. This analysis has been judged weak on the ground that it entails restricting the lawfulness of the beasts of cattle for them to the state of their not making game lawful while they are in iḥrām (consecration), since its meaning becomes: "The beasts of cattle have been made lawful to you in the state of the negation of your making game lawful while you are in iḥrām", whereas the purpose is that the beasts of cattle have been made lawful to them in this state and in others. This is if by «بهيمة الأنعام» the cattle themselves are meant. But if by it are meant the gazelles, the wild asses and the wild cows, as some interpreted it, then a benefit appears in the restriction by this ḥāl, since the meaning becomes: "these things have been made lawful to you in the state of the negation of your making game lawful while you are in iḥrām", and this is a sound meaning; but the construction that I have construed for you has some awkwardness in it. Had this meaning been intended by the noble verse, it would have come in the best and most eloquent construction.

The second analysis — the view of al-Akhfash and a group — is that it is a ḥāl from the agent of «أوْفوا», the implied form being: "fulfil the contracts in the state of the negation of your making game lawful while you are in iḥrām". They judged this school weak in two respects. The first: that it entails separating the ḥāl from the one it describes by a foreign clause, and separation is permissible only by parenthetical clauses; and this clause, namely His saying {أُحِلَّتْ لَكُمْ بَهِيمَةُ الأنعام}, is not parenthetical, but establishes rulings and explains them, whereas a parenthetical clause conveys only emphasis and reinforcement. The second: that it entails restricting the command to fulfil contracts to this state, so the implied form becomes as preceded; and if we consider its implied meaning (mafhūm), the meaning becomes: "if this state is absent, do not fulfil the contracts" — and the matter is not so, for they are commanded to fulfil contracts in every state, in iḥrām and otherwise.

The third analysis: that it is accusative as a ḥāl from the genitive pronoun in «عليكم», i.e. "except what is recited to you in the state of the negation of your making game lawful". This is also weak, for what preceded: what is recited to them is not restricted to this state rather than others; rather it is recited to them in this state and in others.

The fourth analysis: that it is a ḥāl from the implied agent, i.e. the one that was omitted and whose object was put in its place, in His saying {أُحِلَّتْ لَكُمْ بَهِيمَةُ}; for the implied form according to him is: "Allah made lawful to you the beasts of cattle, not making game lawful for you while you are in iḥrām"; then the agent was omitted and He put the object in its place, and left the ḥāl from the agent «[Translator's note: the text has «من الفعل» "from the verb", apparently for «من الفاعل» "from the agent".]» remaining. This analysis is weak in several respects. The first: that the agent replaced [by the deputy agent] has become something utterly forgotten, not paid attention to — they stated this explicitly. If you said «أُنْزِلَ الغيث مجيباً لدعائهم» ("The rain was sent down, answering their prayer"), making «مجيباً» a ḥāl from the replaced agent — the implied form being "Allah sent down the rain while answering their prayer" — it would not be permissible; so likewise this. This is especially so if it is said that the form of the passive verb is an independent form, not derived from the form of the active, as is the view of the Kufans and a group of the Basrans. The second: that it entails restriction by this ḥāl if by «الأنعام» are meant the eight pairs, and restricting His, Exalted is He, making these eight pairs lawful to them to the state of the negation of His making game lawful while they are in iḥrām — whereas Allah the Exalted has made these lawful to them absolutely. The third: that «مُحِلِّي» is written in the plural form, so how could it be a ḥāl from Allah? It is as though this proponent claimed that the word is «مُحِلّ» without yāʾ; and something resembling this view will come.

The fifth analysis: that it is accusative by repeated exception, i.e. that it and His saying «إلا ما يتلى» are two exceptions from one thing, namely «بهيمة الأنعام» «[Translator's note: the text has «بيهمة».]». Some transmitted that from the Basrans; he said: "The implied form is: except what is recited to you, except game while you are in iḥrām — unlike His saying, Exalted is He: {إِنَّآ أُرْسِلْنَآ إلى قَوْمٍ مُّجْرِمِينَ} [al-Ḥijr: 58], as its explanation will come." This proponent said: "Were it so, game would have to be permissible in iḥrām, because it is excepted from the permission. This analysis is to be discarded; so its meaning is: the beasts of cattle have been made lawful to you, you not making game lawful while you are in iḥrām, except what is recited to you other than game." End of quotation.

Al-Shaykh said: "The difficulty only arose from their making «غير محلّي الصيد» a ḥāl from those commanded to fulfil the contracts, or from the One who makes things lawful for them, namely Allah the Exalted, or from those to whom [the prohibitions] are recited. What deceived them in this is that «محلِّي» is written with yāʾ, and they construed it as an active participle of «أحلَّ», annexed to «الصيد» as a transitive active participle is annexed to its object, and as a plural from which the nūn has been deleted for the iḍāfa (genitive construct), its origin being «غيرَ محلين الصيد» — except in the view of the one who made it a ḥāl from the omitted agent, for he does not construe the deletion of a nūn but the deletion of tanwīn. The difficulty disappears and the meaning becomes clear only by taking His saying «مُحِلّي الصيد» to be of the category of their saying «حسان النساء» ('the beautiful of women'), meaning 'the beautiful women'; so likewise this: its origin is 'other than the game that is muḥill', «المُحِلّ» being an adjective of the game, not of the people nor of the omitted agent.

"The game's being described as «مُحِلّ» is in two senses. The first: that it means 'entered the ḥill (the area outside the sanctuary)', as you say «أَحَلَّ الرجلُ» when he enters the ḥill, and «أحرم» when he enters the ḥaram. The second: that it means 'became possessed of lawfulness', i.e. lawful by Allah's making it lawful. That is because game is of two kinds, lawful and unlawful; and «الصيد» in the language of the Arabs is not restricted to the lawful, though it is restricted to it in the Sharīʿa. The Arabs have used it figuratively, applying «الصيد» to what is described neither by lawfulness nor unlawfulness, as in the poet's saying:

168 - 4- لَيْثٌ يعَثَّرَ يصطادُ الرجالَ إذا ... ما الليثُ كَذَّب عن أقرانِه صَدَقَا
(A lion of ʿAththar that hunts men; when the lion flinches from its peers, he holds true.)

and the saying of another:

168 - 5- وقد ذَهَبَتْ سَلْمَى بعقلِك كلِّه ... فهل غيرُ صيدٍ أَحْرَزَتْهُ حبائِلُهْ
(Salmā has carried off your whole mind — are you anything but game that her snares have caught?)

and the saying of Imruʾ al-Qays:

168 - 6- وهِرُّ تصيدُ قلوبَ الرجالِ ... وأَفْلَتَ منها ابنُ عمروٍ حُجُرْ
(And Hirr hunts the hearts of men, yet Ḥujr, son of ʿAmr, escaped her.)

"The occurrence of afʿala in the two senses mentioned is frequent in the speech of the Arabs. Of afʿala for reaching and entering a place is their saying: «أحرمَ الرجلُ», «أَعْرق», «أَشْأَم», «أَيْمن», «أَتْهم» and «أَنْجد», when he reaches these places and alights in them. Of afʿala in the sense of 'became possessed of such-and-such' is their saying: «أعشبت الأرض» (the land became grassy), «أبقلت» (it put forth herbs), «أَغَدَّ البعير» (the camel got a gland-swelling), «أَلْبنت الشاة» (the ewe had milk) and others, «أَجْرت الكلبة» (the bitch had pups), «أَصْرم النخل» (the palms were ready to be cut), «أَتْلَت الناقة» (the she-camel had a following young), «أَحْصَدَ الزرع» (the crop was ready to harvest), «أَجْرب الرجل» (the man's camels got mange), and «أنجبت المرأة» (the woman bore noble children). Once it is established that game is described as «مُحِلّ» in one of the two senses mentioned — having reached the ḥill or having become possessed of lawfulness — it becomes clear that it is a second exception, and not an exception from an exception, since that is impossible because of the contradiction of the ruling: what is excepted from the lawful is unlawful, and what is excepted from the unlawful is lawful.

"Rather, if what is meant by «بهيمة الأنعام» is the cattle themselves, it is a disconnected exception; and if what is meant is the gazelles, wild cows and wild asses, it is a connected exception, according to one of the two interpretations of «المُحِلّ»: He excepted the game that has reached the ḥill while they are in iḥrām. If you say: what is the point of this exception with the restriction of reaching the ḥill, when game in the ḥaram is not lawful either? I say: game in the ḥaram is not lawful for one in iḥrām nor for one not in iḥrām; only game in the ḥill is lawful for one not in iḥrām. So He drew attention that if game in the ḥill is [unlawful] for one in iḥrām — even though it is lawful for others — then game in the ḥaram is all the more fittingly unlawful for him.

"On this interpretation, His saying {إِلاَّ مَا يتلى عَلَيْكُمْ}, if what is meant by it is what comes after it in His saying {حُرِّمَتْ عَلَيْكُمُ} — the verse — is a disconnected exception, since carrion and what is mentioned with it are not specific to gazelles, wild cows and wild asses; so it becomes: 'but what is recited to you — i.e. its prohibition — is unlawful'. And if what is meant by «بهيمة الأنعام» is cattle and wild beasts, the two exceptions refer back to the whole in detail: «ما يتلى عليكم» refers to the eight pairs, and «غيرَ مُحِلّي الصيد» refers to the wild beasts, since the second cannot be an exception from the first exception; and when that is impossible and its reference to the first is possible in some way, it refers to the first. The grammarians have stated that when it is impossible to except some of the excepted items from others, all are made excepted from the first, as in «قام القومُ إلا زيداً إلا عمرواً إلا بكراً» ('The people stood, except Zayd, except ʿAmr, except Bakr').

"If you say: what you mentioned in this explanation — «المُحِلّ» being an attribute of the game, not of the people nor of the omitted agent — is refused by its spelling in the Muṣḥaf, «مُحِلّي» with yāʾ; had it been an attribute of the game rather than the people, «مُحِلّ» would have been written without yāʾ; and the reciters' pausing on it with yāʾ also refuses that. I say: that does not disturb the explanation, because they wrote in the noble Muṣḥaf things contrary to their pronunciation, such as their writing {لأَذْبَحَنَّهُ} [al-Naml: 21] and {ولأَوْضَعُواْ} [al-Tawba: 47] with an alif after the lām-alif; their writing «بأَيْيد» with two yāʾs after the hamza; their writing «أولئك» with an added wāw and a missing alif after the lām; their writing «الصالحات» and the like with the two alifs dropped; and other such things. As for their pausing on it with yāʾ, it is not permissible, since one does not pause on the muḍāf without the muḍāf ilayhi; if someone pauses, it is only because of running out of breath or for testing. Moreover, its writing with yāʾ and pausing on it with yāʾ can be accounted for: in the dialect of al-Azd they pause on «بزيدٍ» as «بزيدي», changing the tanwīn to yāʾ; so «مُحِلِّي» was written according to pausal form in this dialect, with yāʾ. This is an accounting for an orthographic anomaly, and the orthography of the Muṣḥaf is not a basis for analogy." End of quotation.

What he mentioned and chose, and for which he declared people to be in error, is worthless. What he mentioned in accounting for the presence of the yāʾ in writing and in pause is a sheer error: for even granting that in that dialect, where is the tanwīn in «مُحِل»? How can it have tanwīn when it is a muḍāf, so that he can say it may be accounted for by the dialect of al-Azd? And what he mentioned — that it may be among what they wrote as they wrote those examples mentioned — is not to be relied upon, because the writing of the Muṣḥaf is a followed practice (sunna) that is not a basis for analogy; so how can he say that this may be compared with those things? Moreover, they did not parse «غير» except as a ḥāl, to the point that some transmitted consensus on that; they disagreed only about the one it describes. So his saying that it is a second exception, together with these weak analyses, breaches the consensus — except for what was transmitted above from some that it is a second exception, which he attributed to the Basrans, but not on the basis of the reasoning al-Shaykh mentioned.

In old times and new, people have found this verse difficult. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "People have confused matters in this place regarding the accusative of «غير», and construed frontings and postponings, all of which is unsatisfactory, because the speech runs regularly, so an exception after an exception is possible." This verse is one whose eloquence and rhetorical excellence has been evident to the eloquent and the rhetoricians, so much so that it is related that al-Kindī was told: "O sage, compose for us the like of this Qurʾān." He said: "Yes, I will compose for you the like of part of it." He secluded himself for many days, then came out and said: "By Allah, no one is able to do that. I opened the Muṣḥaf and Sūrat al-Māʾida came out, and there it had spoken of fidelity, forbidden breaking [covenants], made lawful in general, then made an exception after an exception, then told of His power and wisdom — in two lines."

The majority read «غير» in the accusative; Ibn Abī ʿAbla read it in the nominative, and there are two analyses. The more apparent: that it is an adjective of «بهيمة الأنعام»; and what is qualified by «غير» need not be of the same kind as what follows it — you say: «مررت برجلٍ غير حمار» ("I passed by a man, not a donkey"). So they said; and there is a reservation about it, but the apparent sense of this reading supports them. The second: that it is an adjective of the pronoun in «يُتْلى». Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "Because «غير محلي الصيد» is in meaning on a par with 'not made lawful when it is game'"; and there is strain in it.

«الصيد» is originally the maṣdar (verbal noun) of «صاد يصيد ويُصاد», and it is applied to what is hunted, as in «درهمٌ ضَرْبُ الأميرِ» ("a dirham, the emir's striking", i.e. struck by the emir). In the noble verse it admits both: remaining a maṣdar, as if it were said "He has made the beasts of cattle lawful to you, you not making hunting lawful while you are in iḥrām"; and standing in place of the object, i.e. "you not making the hunted thing lawful while you are in iḥrām".

His saying: {وَأَنْتُمْ حُرُمٌ}: a mubtadaʾ (subject) and khabar (predicate) in the position of the accusative as a ḥāl. What is the one described by this ḥāl? Al-Zamakhsharī said: "It is a ḥāl from «مُحِلّي الصيد», as if it were said: We have made lawful to you some of the cattle while you refrain from game, being in iḥrām, lest We impose hardship on you." Al-Shaykh said: "We have shown the unsoundness of this view, in that the cattle are permissible absolutely, not by restriction to this state." This rejoinder is worthless, because if He made some of the cattle lawful to them while they refrain from game, then that He should make them lawful to them when they are not in iḥrām is all the more so. «حُرُم» is the plural of «حرام» in the sense of «مُحْرِم»; the poet said:

168 - 7- فقلْتُ هلا فيئي إليك فإنني ... حَرَامُ وإني بعد ذاك لبيبُ
(So I said: Hold! Turn yourself away, for I am in iḥrām, and I am moreover one who answers the call [labbayk].)

i.e. «مُلَبٍّ» (one pronouncing the talbiya). «أَحْرَمَ» is said when one enters the ḥaram or enters iḥrām. Makkī ibn Abī Ṭālib said: "It is in the position of the accusative as a ḥāl from the pronoun implied in «محلي»." This is the correct view. As for what Abū al-Qāsim [al-Zamakhsharī] mentioned, it is not apparent, and it involves the ḥāl coming from the muḍāf ilayhi outside the excepted cases.

Yaḥyā ibn Waththāb, Ibrāhīm and al-Ḥasan read «حُرْم» with the rāʾ vowelless. Abū al-Ḥasan said: "It is the dialect of Tamīm", meaning that they make vowelless the ḍamma of the plural fuʿul, as in «رُسْل».

semin-durr:47-47.t:
His saying, Exalted is He: {وَلْيَحْكُمْ}: the majority read it with a sukūn on the lām and the verb after it in the jussive (majzūm), on the basis that it is the lām of command, given a sukūn by analogy with «كَتْف» (shoulder), even though its original vowel is a kasra; some read it with this original [kasra]. Ḥamza — may Allah have mercy on him — read it with a kasra and the verb after it in the accusative, making it the lām of purpose (lām kay), so he put the verb after it in the accusative by a concealed «أن», as has been established more than once. On the reading of the majority and the anomalous reading it is a resumptive sentence. On Ḥamza's reading, the lām may be attached to «آتينا» or to «قَفَّيْنا» if we make «هدى وموعظة» objects of purpose (mafʿūl lahu), i.e. "We sent [him] following for guidance and admonition and for judging," or "We gave him [the Injīl] for guidance, admonition and judging." If we make the two of them circumstantials conjoined to «مصدقاً», then «وليحكم» in his reading is attached to an omitted element indicated by the wording, as though it were said: "and for judging We gave him that."

al-Zamakhsharī said: "If you say: if you string «هدى وموعظة» on the same thread as «مصدقاً», what do you do with His saying «وليحكم»? I say: I do with it what I did with «هدى وموعظة» when I made them objects of purpose, and I assume: 'and so that the people of the Injīl may judge by what Allah sent down, We gave it to him'." Ibn ʿAṭiyya said something close to the first view — I mean «وليحكم» being an object of purpose conjoined to «هدى», with the governor being the expressed «آتيناه» — for he said: "And We gave him the Injīl so that it might contain guidance, light and confirmation, and so that the people of the Injīl might judge." The Shaykh [Abū Ḥayyān] said: "So he conjoined «وليحكم» to a supposed cause, which is why he said 'so that it might contain'." The Shaykh mentioned al-Zamakhsharī's previous statement and considered it closer to correctness than Ibn ʿAṭiyya's statement. He said: "Because the first guidance, the light and the confirmation were not brought as a cause; His saying {فِيهِ هُدًى وَنُورٌ} was brought only in the sense of 'that being in it, and confirming', and this is the meaning of the ḥāl (circumstantial), and a ḥāl is not a cause. So his saying 'so that it might contain such-and-such, and so that … might judge' is far-fetched."

The first verse was closed with «الكافرون», the second with «الظالمون» and the third with «الفاسقون» for reasons of appropriateness that people have mentioned. The best that has been said about it is what al-Shaʿbī mentioned: that the first concerns the Muslims, the second the Jews, and the third the Christians. That is because before the first [come] «فإنْ جاؤوك فاحكُمْ», «وكيف يُحَكِّمونك» and «يَحْكُم بها النبيون»; before the second, «وكَتَبْنا عليهم», and they are the Jews; and before the third, «وليحكم أهل الإنجيل», and they are the Christians. So it is as though He assigned each one to what precedes it. Ubayy read «وأن ليحكم» with an added «أن», and this is not a place where it is added.

semin-durr:48-48.t:
His saying, Exalted is He: {بالحق}: the bāʾ may be [the head of] a ḥāl (circumstantial) from «الكتاب», i.e. clothed in truth and veracity, and it is a corroborative ḥāl; or it may be a ḥāl from the agent, i.e. "accompanied by the truth"; or a ḥāl from the kāf in «إليك», i.e. "while you are clothed in the truth." The parallel of «من الكتاب» has been given. «أل» in the first «الكتاب» is that of prior reference (ʿahd), and it is the Quran, without disagreement. In the second it may be generic, since what is meant is the heavenly scriptures. The Shaykh [Abū Ḥayyān] allowed it to be that of prior reference, since what is meant is a known kind of scripture, not everything to which this name applies. The difference between the two views is that the first requires the omission of an adjective, i.e. "the divine scripture," while the second does not need that, because the prior reference in the noun includes it with all its attributes.

His saying: {وَمُهَيْمِناً}: the majority read it with a kasra on the second mīm, as an active participle. It is a ḥāl from the first «الكتاب», because it is conjoined to the ḥāl from it, namely «مصدقاً». «مصدقاً» and «مهيمناً» may also both be circumstantials from the kāf of «إليك»; this will be examined when the reading of Mujāhid, may Allah have mercy on him, is mentioned. «عليه» is attached to «مهيمِن». «المهيمِن» is the watcher; [the poet] said:

1733 - إنَّ الكتابَ مهيمِنٌ لنبيِّنا ... والحقُّ يعرِفُه ذَوُو الأَلْبابِ
(The Book is a guardian-witness for our Prophet, and the truth is recognised by those of understanding.)

It also means the preserver; [the poet] said:

1734 - مليكٌ على عرشِ السماء مهيمِنٌ ... لعزته تَعْنُو الوجوهُ وتَسْجُدُ
(A King upon the throne of heaven, Watchful Guardian; to His might faces humble themselves and prostrate.)

It is also the witness. They disagreed about it: is it an original form in itself, i.e. not substituted from anything? One says «هَيْمَن يُهَيْمن فهو مُهَيْمِن», like «بَيْطَر يُبَيْطِر فهو مُبَيْطِر» (to practise farriery). Abū ʿUbayda said: "Only four words have come in the speech of the Arabs on this pattern: «مُبَيْطِر», «مُسَيْطِر», «مُهَيْمِن» and «مُحَيْمِر»." Abū al-Qāsim al-Zajjājī, in his commentary on the preface of Adab al-Kātib, added a fifth word, namely «مُبَيْقِر», the active participle of «بَيْقَر يُبَيْقِر», i.e. he went out from one horizon to another, or [from] «البُقَّيْرى», a game well known among children. It is also said that its hāʾ is substituted for a hamza and that it is the active participle of «آمنَ غيرَه من الخوف» (he made another safe from fear), the original being «مُأَأْمِن» with two hamzas; the second was changed to yāʾ out of dislike of two hamzas together, then the first was changed to hāʾ, as in «هراق», «هَراح» and «هَبَرْتُ الثوب» for «أراق», «أراح» and «أَبَرْتُ الثوب». This is weak, or involves an unnecessary strain, especially since it has patterns to which it can be assimilated, such as «مُبَيْطِر» and its sisters. Moreover, the [second] hamza of «مُأَأْمِن», the active participle of «آمن», is by rule elided, so it cannot be claimed that it was retained and then changed to hāʾ; this is something without parallel.

Ibn Qutayba fell into a gross error when he claimed that «مُهَيْمِناً» is a diminutive, and that its original is «مُؤَيْمِن», the diminutive of the active participle «مُؤْمن», whose hamza was then changed to hāʾ as in «هَراق». This is also attributed to Abū al-ʿAbbās al-Mubarrad. However, al-Zajjāj said: "This is good according to the method of Arabic, and it agrees with what came in the exegesis that the meaning of «مُهَيْمن» is «مُؤْمن» (one who grants safety)." This which al-Zajjāj said [and approved, people objected to against him, against al-Mubarrad and those who followed them]. When this statement reached Abū al-ʿAbbās Thaʿlab he objected to it most vehemently, attacked Ibn Qutayba and wrote to him: "Fear Allah, for this is disbelief or something like it," because the names of Allah the Exalted are not put in the diminutive, nor is any name held in reverence by the Law. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "al-Naqqāsh related that when that reached Thaʿlab he said: 'What Ibn Qutayba said is bad and false, and assailing the Quran is grave. He never heard ḥadīth from a strong [transmitter] or a weak one; he only compiled books out of an obsession that overcame him'." [Abū al-Baqāʾ said: "The original of «مُهَيْمن» is «مُؤَيْمِن», because it is derived from «الأمانة» (trust), since the muhaymin is the witness; and «هَيْمن» does not exist in the language so that the hāʾ could be original." What he said is worthless, because of what was related above from the lexicographers about «هَيْمَن».] [Translator's note: the source reads «لي بشيء», evidently for «ليس بشيء».] The most that can be said on the matter is that they used it only with the yāʾ added, like «بَيْطَر» and its class.

Ibn Muḥayṣin and Mujāhid read «ومُهَيْمَنا» with a fatḥa on the second mīm, as a passive participle, in the sense that it is guarded from alteration and change, the agent being Allah the Exalted: {إِنَّا نَحْنُ نَزَّلْنَا الذكر وَإِنَّا لَهُ لَحَافِظُونَ} [al-Ḥijr: 9]; or [by] someone who guards it in every land, so that if a vowel of it is altered people notice it and correct the reciter. On this reading the pronoun in «عليه» refers to the first «الكتاب», and on the well-known reading it refers to the second «الكتاب». Ibn Abī Najīḥ related from Mujāhid his reading with a fatḥa, and he said: "Its meaning is: Muḥammad is entrusted with the Quran." al-Ṭabarī said: "On this view «مهيمناً» is a ḥāl from the kāf in «إليك»," and he challenged this view because of the presence of the wāw in «ومهيمنا», since it is conjoined to «مصدقاً», and «مصدقاً» is a ḥāl from «الكتاب», not a ḥāl from the kāf; for if it were a ḥāl from it, the construction would be «لما بين يديك» with the kāf.

The Shaykh said: "Interpreting it as a shift (iltifāt) from address to the third person is far from the style of the Quran, and assuming 'and We made you, O Muḥammad, a guardian' is farther still," meaning that these two interpretations could serve as answers about Mujāhid's statement, but the first is far-fetched and the second more far-fetched than it. Here Ibn ʿAṭiyya, after relating Mujāhid's reading and his explanation that Muḥammad, upon him be peace, is the trustee of the Quran, said: "al-Ṭabarī said: on this view His saying «ومهيمناً» is a ḥāl from the kāf in His saying «إليك»; he said: and this is an interpretation far from what is understood." [Ibn ʿAṭiyya] said: "al-Ṭabarī erred concerning this word against Mujāhid, for he explained his interpretation according to the reading of the people, «مهيمِناً» with a kasra on the second mīm, and so the interpretation became far-fetched. But Mujāhid — Allah's mercy be upon him — and Ibn Muḥayṣin read «ومهيمَنا» with a fatḥa on the second mīm, which is the passive participle form, and it is a ḥāl from «الكتاب» conjoined to His saying «مصدقاً». On this, it follows that the one entrusted with it is Muḥammad, upon him be peace." He said: "And Makkī, may Allah have mercy on him, proceeded likewise." I say: what Abū Muḥammad [Ibn ʿAṭiyya] said contains nothing that refutes al-Ṭabarī, for al-Ṭabarī found it problematic that «مهيمنا» be a ḥāl from the kāf on Mujāhid's reading. Furthermore, Ibn ʿAṭiyya said after that: "«مصدقاً ومهيمناً» may be two circumstantials from the kāf in «إليك», and this is not peculiar to the reading of Mujāhid alone, as Makkī claimed." People found it problematic that they be two circumstantials from the kāf of «إليك» only because of the awkwardness of the construction; what is wrong with it and the two interpretations transmitted by the Shaykh have been given. His saying "this is not peculiar …" is a correct statement, even though Makkī adhered to it, and it is the evident [reading of his words].

«عليه» is in the position of the nominative on the reading of Ibn Muḥayṣin and Mujāhid, because it stands in place of the agent; so said Ibn ʿAṭiyya. I say: this is if we make «مهيمناً» a ḥāl from «الكتاب». But if we make it a ḥāl from the kāf of «إليك», then what stands in place of the agent is a latent pronoun referring to the Prophet, upon him be peace, and «عليه» is then in the position of the accusative, just as if it were read as an active participle.

His saying: {عَمَّا جَآءَكَ}: there are two views. First — and Abū al-Baqāʾ held it —: it is a ḥāl, i.e. "turning away from what has come to you." This is open to question, in that «عن» is an incomplete preposition that does not occur as the khabar (predicate) of a concrete noun, and so likewise does not occur as a ḥāl from it; an incomplete preposition is attached only to a general [notion of] being, not to a specific one, and a specific one may not be omitted. Second: «عَنْ» has its proper sense of passing beyond, but with «تَتَّبعْ» implying the meaning of «تتزَحْزَحْ وتنحرف» (budge and deviate), i.e. "do not deviate [from it], following."

His saying: {مِنَ الحق}: there are also two views on it. First: it is a ḥāl from the nominative pronoun in «جاءك». Second: it is a ḥāl from the relative «ما» itself, so it is attached to an omitted element. It may also be explicative.

His saying «لكل»: «كل» is annexed to something omitted. That omitted element may be the word «أمة», i.e. "for every community," meaning by them all people — Muslims, Jews and Christians; or that omitted element may be «الأنبياء», i.e. "for all the prophets mentioned above." «جَعَلْنا» may be transitive to two objects, meaning "We made," so that «لكل» is a fronted object and «شِرْعة» a second object. His saying {منكم} is attached to an omitted element, i.e. "I mean: of you." It may not be attached to an omitted element as an adjective of «كل», for two reasons. First: it would entail separating the adjective from what it qualifies by His saying «جَعَلْنا», which is an extraneous clause containing neither emphasis nor reinforcement, and what is like that may not separate. Second: it would entail separating «جَعَلْنا» from what it governs, namely «شِرْعةً». So said Abū al-Baqāʾ, and it is open to question, for what governs «لكل» is not extraneous. This is shown by His saying {أَغَيْرَ الله أَتَّخِذُ وَلِيّاً فَاطِرِ} [al-Anʿām: 14], where He separated the Divine Name from its adjective by what governs the first object; and this is its parallel.

Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī and Yaḥyā ibn Waththāb read «شَرْعة» with a fatḥa on the shīn, as though the kasra form is for the manner and the fatḥa form a maṣdar (verbal noun).

«الشِرْعة» originally means the established practice (sunna); from it: {شَرَعَ لَكُم مِّنَ الدين} [al-Shūrā: 13], i.e. He laid down as practice. «الشارع» is the road, and it is from «الشريعة», which originally is the path leading to water; from it is his saying:

1735 - وفي الشرائعِ منْ جِلاَّنَ مُقْتَنِصٌ ... بالي الثيابِ خَفيُّ الصوتِ مُنْزَرِبُ
(And at the watering-paths of Jillān there is a hunter, worn of clothes, low of voice, hidden in his lair.)

«المِنْهاج» is derived from «الطريق النَّهْج», the clear road; from it is his saying:

1736 - مَنْ يَكُ ذا شَكٍّ فهذا فَلْجُ ... ماءٌ رُواءٌ وطريقٌ نَهْجُ
(Whoever is in doubt — this is a stream: water that quenches and a clear road.)

i.e. clear. One says «طريق مَنْهَجٌ» and «نَهْجٌ». Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "«مِنْهاج» is an intensive form from «نَهَج»," meaning like their saying «إنه لمِنْحارٌ بوائكَها» (he is one who slaughters much of its fat she-camels); and this is good. Are «الشرعة» and «المنهاج» of one meaning, as in his saying:

1737 - . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ... وهند أتى مِنْ دونِها النَّأْيُ والبُعْدُ
(… and Hind — distance and remoteness have come between [us and] her.)

[and as in his saying:]

1738 - . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ... وأَلْفَى قولَها كَذِباً ومَيْنا
(… and he found her words to be lies and falsehood.)

or do they differ? [On the latter view,] «الشِّرْعة» is the beginning of the road and «المِنْهاج» the continuing road — so said al-Mubarrad; or «الشِرْعة» is the road whether clear or unclear, and «المنهاج» only the clear road, so the first is more general — so said Ibn al-Anbārī; or [they are] the religion and the proof? It is a well-known disagreement.

His saying: {ولكن لِّيَبْلُوَكُمْ}: attached to an omitted element. Abū al-Baqāʾ assumed it as "but He divided you in order to test you," and others assumed it as "but He did not will to make you one community," and this is better, because the wording and meaning indicate it. «جميعاً» is a ḥāl from «كم» in «مرجعكم». What governs this ḥāl is either the maṣdar annexed to «كم» — for «كم» may be an agent, the maṣdar resolving into a maṣdar particle and an active verb, the original being "you return all together"; or it may be the deputy agent (mafʿūl lam yusamma fāʿiluhu), on the basis that the maṣdar resolves into a passive verb, i.e. "Allah returns you" [Translator's note: the source writes «معفولاً» for «مفعولاً»]; and both meanings have been stated explicitly in [various] places — or it is governed by the implied [notion of] being established in the prepositional phrase, namely «إليه». «إليه مَرْجِعُكم» may be of the category of verbal clauses or of nominal clauses; this is clear from what was said on its parallels. «فَيُنَبِّئُكم» here is from «نَبَّأ» not implying the meaning of «أعلم» (to inform [with three objects]), and therefore it is transitive to one object by itself and to the other by a preposition.

semin-durr:49-49.t:
His saying, Exalted is He: {وَأَنِ احكم}: there are four views on it. First: its position is accusative, conjoined to «الكتاب», i.e. "and We sent down to you the judging." Second: it is in the position of the genitive, conjoined to «بالحق», i.e. "We sent it down with the truth and with the judging"; on this view the position of «أَنْ» may be accusative or genitive, according to the well-known disagreement. Third: it is in the position of the nominative as a mubtadaʾ (subject), and in assuming its khabar (predicate) there are two possibilities. One: that you assume it after it, i.e. "your judging by what Allah sent down is Our command" or "Our saying." The other: that you assume it before it, i.e. "and among what is obligatory is that you judge," i.e. your judging. Fourth: it is explicative (tafsīriyya). Abū al-Baqāʾ said: "This is far-fetched, because the wāw prevents it, and the meaning invalidates it, since the explicative «أَنْ» ought to be preceded by a saying which is explained by it." As for what he mentioned about the wāw preventing «أَنْ» from being explicative, it is clear. As for his saying "preceded by a saying," its correction is to say "by what has the meaning of saying, but not its letters." Then he said: "This view could be made correct by assuming 'And We commanded you', and then this command is explained by «احكم»." The Shaykh [Abū Ḥayyān] rejected making this view correct by what Abū al-Baqāʾ mentioned; he said: "Because the omission of the clause explained by «أَنْ» and what follows it is not preserved from their language." And it is as he said.

The two readings with a ḍamma on the nūn of «أن» and with a kasra on it are clear from what was said in al-Baqara: the ḍamma is for vowel harmony and the kasra is according to the basic rule for the meeting of two quiescent letters. The pronoun in «بينهم» is either for the Jews specifically or for all those who seek judgement.

His saying: {أَن يَفْتِنُوكَ}: there are two views on it. The more evident: it is a mafʿūl li-ajlihi (object of purpose) [Translator's note: the source writes «معفولٌ» for «مفعولٌ»], i.e. "beware of them for fear that they tempt you." Second: it is a badal (substitute) of the object, by way of inclusion (ishtimāl), as though [He said]: "and beware of them — their temptation," as in your saying «أعجبني زيدٌ علمُه» (Zayd pleased me — his knowledge).

His saying: {فَإِن تَوَلَّوْاْ}: Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "Before it there is an omission indicated by the apparent [text], its implied form being: do not follow, and beware; then if they seek your judgement despite that and are upright with you, how excellent that is; but if they turn away, then know …" It would be good to assume this omitted counterpart after His saying «لفاسقون». What ought to be said is that in this type there is no omission, because it is of the category of what is implied by the address (faḥwā al-khiṭāb), and the matter is clear.

semin-durr:29-29.t: His saying, Exalted is He: {إني أُرِيدُ أَن تَبُوءَ}: there are three interpretations of it. One of them: that it is on the omission of the interrogative hamza, its implied form being «أإني أريد» ("do I intend …?"); it is an interrogative of denial, because intending disobedience is ugly, and from the prophets it is uglier, and they are protected from that. This interpretation is supported by the reading of those who read «أنَّى أريد» with fatḥa on the nūn; it is «أنَّى» in the sense of «كيف», i.e. how could I intend that? The second: that «لا» is omitted, its implied form being «إني أريدُ أن لا تبوء» ("I intend that you not bear …"), like His saying, Exalted is He: {يُبَيِّنُ الله لَكُمْ أَن تَضِلُّواْ} [al-Nisāʾ: 176] and {رَوَاسِيَ أَن تَمِيدَ بِكُمْ} [al-Naḥl: 15], i.e. "lest you go astray" and "lest it shake"; this is widespread. This too is an escape from affirming the intention for him. Some weakened this interpretation by his saying, upon him be peace: "No soul is killed wrongfully but that the first son of Adam bears a share of its blood, because he was the first to establish killing as a practice"; so by this it is established that the sin occurs. What he weakened it with is not binding, because the one who holds this view says: his not intending the sin for his brother does not entail the absence of the sin; rather he may intend its absence and yet it occurs. The third: that the intending remains as it is; it is either a figurative or a real intention, according to the disagreement of the exegetes on that. The intention of that on his part came for reasons they have mentioned, among them that indications appeared to him showing that his term was near and that his brother was a disbeliever, and intending punishment for a disbeliever is good. His saying «بإثمي» is in the position of the accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial) from the agent of «تَبُوء», i.e. you return carrying it and clothed with it; its parallel has preceded in His saying {فَبَآءُو بِغَضَبٍ} [al-Baqara: 90]. They said: a muḍāf is necessary. Al-Zamakhsharī supposed it as "with the like of my sin", and said: "by way of latitude in speech, as you say: I read the reading of so-and-so, and I wrote his writing"; and some supposed it as "with the sin of killing me". His saying {وَذَلِكَ جَزَآءُ} may be part of his speech, or part of the speech of Allah the Exalted.

semin-durr:30-30.t:
His saying, Exalted is He: {فَطَوَّعَتْ}: the majority read «طَوَّعت» with a doubled wāw and without alif, in the sense of "made easy and prompted". Al-Zamakhsharī said: "It made it broad and easy for him, from «طاع له المرتعُ» ('the pasture became ample for him') when it is broad." End of quotation. The doubling in it is for transitivity, because the basic form is «طاعَ له قتلُ أخيه», i.e. the killing of his brother became compliant to him, from «الطواعية» (compliance); then it was made transitive by doubling, so that the agent became an object, as it does with the hamza. Al-Ḥasan, Zayd ibn ʿAlī and a large group read «فطاوعت». Al-Zamakhsharī put forward two possibilities for it. One of them: that it is among the cases in which fāʿala comes not for participation between two things, but in the sense of faʿʿala, as in «ضاعفتُه» and «ضَعَّفْته», and «ناعمته» and «نَعَّمْتُه»; these two examples are among Sībawayh's examples. He [Sībawayh] said: "They brought it on the pattern of «عاقَبْتُه»." He said: "Fāʿaltu may come without your meaning by it the action of two, but they built the verb on it as they built it on afʿaltu", and he mentioned examples, among them «عافاه الله» ("may Allah grant him well-being"). Few have mentioned that fāʿala comes in the sense of faʿʿaltu. "The second possibility: that it has its proper sense of participation, namely that the killing of his brother is as though it invited his soul to undertake it, and his soul complied with it." End of quotation. The clarification of the wording here is to say: He made the killing invite [him] to itself because of the envy that befell Qābīl, and made the soul refuse that and recoil from it; so each of the two — I mean the killing and the soul — is as though it wants its counterpart to obey it, until the killing overcame the soul and the soul complied with it.

«له» is attached to (mutaʿalliq) «طَوَّعت» in both readings. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "And «له» is for additional linkage, as in your saying «حَفِظْتُ لزيدٍ مالَه» ('I guarded Zayd's wealth for him')." He means that the speech would be complete in itself were it said «فَطَوَّعَتْ نفسُه قتلَ أخيه», just as it is in your saying «حَفِظْتُ مالَ زيد»; so He brought this lām for the strength of the speech's linkage. Abū al-Baqāʾ said: "Some people said: «طاوَعَتْ» is transitive without the lām. This is a mistake, because the one that is transitive without the lām is transitive to a single object, and here He made it transitive to «قَتْل أخيه». It was also said: the implied form is «طاوعَتْه نفسُه على قَتْلِ أخيه» ('his soul complied with him in killing his brother'), so He added the lām and omitted «على»." That is, He added the lām in the mafʿūl bihi (direct object), namely the hāʾ, and omitted «على», the preposition governing «قتل أخيه».

semin-durr:31-31.t:
His saying, Exalted is He: {لِيُرِيَهُ كَيْفَ يُوَارِي}: two views are permissible on this lām. One of them: that it is attached to (mutaʿalliq) «يبحث», i.e. it digs and stirs up the earth in order to show. The second: that it is attached to «بَعَثَ». «كيف» is governed by «يُوارِي», and the interrogative clause suspends (muʿalliqa) the visual "seeing", so it is in the position of the second object, standing in its place; because visual «رأى», before it is made transitive by the hamza, is transitive to one object, and by the hamza it acquired another. Its parallel has preceded in His saying: {أَرِنِي كَيْفَ تُحْيِي الموتى} [al-Baqara: 260]. By «السَّوْءَة» here is meant what it is not permissible to uncover of his body; it also means disgrace. He said:

171 - 6-. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ... يالقَومي لِلسَّوْءَة السَّوْآءِ
(… O my people, for the foulest disgrace!)

It may be lightened by throwing the vowel of the hamza onto the wāw, which is the reading of al-Zuhrī; in that case it is not permissible to change this wāw into alif, even though it is true of it that it is a voweled weak letter with a fatḥa before it, because its vowel is accidental. Similar to it are «جَيَل» and «تَوَم», the lightened forms of «جَيْئَل» and «تَوْءَم». It is also permissible to change this hamza into wāw and assimilate what precedes it into it, treating the radical letter like the augment; this is a dialect form: they say «شيّ» and «ضوّ» for «شيء» and «ضوء». He said:

171 - 7- وإنْ يَرَاوسَيَّةً طاروا بها فَرحاً ... مني وما سَمِعُوا من صالحٍ دفَنُوا
(If they see an evil deed of mine they fly off with it in joy, and whatever good they hear [of me] they bury)

Abū Jaʿfar read according to this view.

His saying: {يَاوَيْلَتَا}: the yāʾ of the first person was changed into alif, and this is a widespread dialect form in the vocative annexed to it; it is one of the six dialect forms, whose mention has preceded. It was also read in the same way according to the basic form, which is the reading of al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī. [Translator's note: the wording is as in the source; presumably «يا ويلتي» with the yāʾ is meant.] Although the vocative is originally for one from whom turning towards [the caller] is possible, namely rational beings, the Arabs use it figuratively and call upon what is not rational; the meaning is: "O my woe, be present, for this is the time of your presence". Similar to it are {ياحسرة عَلَى العباد} [Yā Sīn: 30] and {ياحسرتا على مَا فَرَّطَتُ} [al-Zumar: 56]. Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, and Abū ʿAmr in the transmission of al-Dūrī, gave imāla (inclination towards ē) to the alif of «حسرتا». The majority read «أعَجَزْتُ» with fatḥa on the jīm, which is the most eloquent dialect: one says «عَجَزت» — with fatḥa in the past — «أعجِزُ», with kasra in the imperfect. Al-Ḥasan, al-Fayyāḍ, Ibn Masʿūd and Ṭalḥa read it with kasra, which is a minor anomalous dialect form; what is well known is only to say «عَجِزت المرأة» with kasra, i.e. her buttocks became large. «أن أكون» is on the dropping of the preposition, i.e. «عَنْ أكونَ» ("from being"); since it was omitted, the well-known disagreement applies to it.

His saying: {فَأُوَارِيَ}: the majority read it with the accusative on the yāʾ, and there are two explanations of it. The more correct of them: that it is conjoined to «أكونَ», which is made accusative by «أَنْ», falling into its series, i.e. "am I unable to be like the crow and so [be one who] hides?" The second — and al-Zamakhsharī mentioned no other —: that it is accusative as the answer to the interrogative in his saying «أعجَزْتُ», meaning that it would belong to the category of His saying: {فَهَل لَّنَا مِن شُفَعَآءَ فَيَشْفَعُواْ لَنَآ} [al-Aʿrāf: 53]. What Abū al-Qāsim [al-Zamakhsharī] mentioned was rejected by Abū al-Baqāʾ after he related it from some people. He said: "Some mentioned that it may be accusative as the answer to the interrogative, but this is nothing, since the meaning is not: 'will there be inability from me, and then hiding?' Do you not see that your saying «أين بيتُك فأزورَك» ('where is your house, that I may visit you?') means: if I knew, I would visit; whereas the meaning here is not: if I were unable, I would hide." I say: this rejection is correct on its face. The expansion of Abū al-Baqāʾ's wording is that the grammarians stipulate, for the permissibility of making the verb accusative by an implied «أنْ» after the eight things — other than negation — that the speech be resolvable into a condition and a requital; if a condition and a requital can be formed from it, the accusative is sound, otherwise it is impossible. Of this is «أين بيتك فأزورَك», i.e. if you show me your house I will visit you. In this place, if a condition and a requital were resolved from it, the meaning would be corrupted, since the implied form would become "if I am unable, I will hide", and this is not correct, because if he is unable, how would he hide?

The Shaykh [Abū Ḥayyān] refuted Abū al-Qāsim with what has preceded and made it a gross error — and he was preceded in it, as you have seen; so he was discourteous towards him over something he transmitted from someone else; Allah knows best its correctness.

Al-Fayyāḍ ibn Ghazwān and Ṭalḥa ibn Muṣarrif read with sukūn on the yāʾ. Al-Zamakhsharī explained it in one of two ways: either as a break [from what precedes], i.e. "so I will hide", or as giving sukūn in the place of the accusative for lightness. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "It is a minor dialect form, because of the succession of vowels." The Shaykh said: "It is not right to justify the reading by this as long as an alternative is found, since giving sukūn in place of the fatḥa is not permissible except under poetic necessity; and moreover there is no succession of vowels."

His saying: {فَأَصْبَحَ} is in the sense of «صار» ("became"). Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "His saying «فأصبح» is an expression for all his times; part of the time was put in place of the whole of it. The morning was singled out for that because it is the beginning of the day and of setting out to affairs, and the likely time of energy. Of this is the saying of al-Rabīʿ:

171 - 8- أصبحتُ لا أحملُ السلاح ولا ... . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
(I have come to be one who does not carry weapons, nor …)

and the saying of Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ: 'Then the Banū Asad came to reproach me over Islam', and other examples." The Shaykh said: "This justification he mentioned — that «أصبح» is an expression for all his times and that the morning was singled out only because it is the beginning of the day — is not good, because the Arabs used «أضحى», «بات» and «أمسى» in the sense of «صار», and none of them is the beginning of the day." How can it be fitting to refute Abū Muḥammad [Ibn ʿAṭiyya] with something like this? He did not say that because it was put in place of his times for the reason he mentioned, it is in the sense of «صار», such that its sisters would bind him with what [the Shaykh] used to refute him.

semin-durr:111-111.t:
The words of Allah the Exalted: {أَنْ آمِنُواْ}: there are two aspects concerning «أَنْ». The more apparent of them: that it is explicative (tafsīriyya), because it came after something that has the meaning of saying, not its letters. The second: that it is maṣdariyya (forming a verbal noun), by a forced interpretation, i.e. "I enjoined upon them the command to believe". Here they said «آمنَّا» without mentioning what is believed in, whereas there [they said] {آمَنَّا بالله} [Āl ʿImrān: 52], mentioning it. The difference is that there only Allah the Exalted had been mentioned before, so what is believed in was repeated and it was said «بالله»; while here two things were mentioned before that, namely {أَنْ آمِنُواْ بِي وَبِرَسُولِي}, so it was not mentioned, in order to include both things mentioned. There is a point to consider in this. Here [it is] «بأنَّنا», while there «بأنَّا» with the omission; it has been stated more than once that this [the full form] is the original. The original was brought here only because what is believed in is multiple, so emphasis suited it.

His words: {هَلْ يَسْتَطِيعُ}: the majority read «يَسْتَطيع» with the yāʾ of the third person and «ربك» in the nominative as fāʿil (agent). Al-Kisāʾī read «تَسْتَطيع» with the tāʾ of address to ʿĪsā, and «ربَّك» in the accusative, with reverence; his rule is to assimilate the lām of «هل» into certain letters, among them this place. ʿĀʾisha read with al-Kisāʾī's reading, and she used to say: "The disciples knew Allah better than to say: Is your Lord able?" It is as though she — may Allah be pleased with her — declared them free of having this hideous statement attributed to them. Muʿādh also read thus, as did ʿAlī, Ibn ʿAbbās and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr among others. Then they disagreed about this reading: does it need the omission of a muḍāf or not? The majority of parsers assume: "Are you able to ask your Lord?" Al-Fārisī said: "It may be possible to dispense with assuming «سؤالَ» (asking), the meaning being: are you able [to bring it about] that your Lord sends down by your supplication; so the meaning is referred — necessarily — to something implied which the wording mentioned indicates." The Shaykh said: "What he said is not apparent, because His act, the Exalted, though caused by the supplication, is not within ʿĪsā's power." Abū ʿUbayd chose this reading, saying: "because the other reading resembles the disciples being doubters, whereas this one does not give that impression." I say: this is people building on the premise that they were believers, and this is the truth.

Ibn al-Anbārī said: "It is not permissible for anyone to imagine of the disciples that they doubted the power of Allah the Exalted." By this it becomes apparent that al-Zamakhsharī's statement that they were not believers is not good; it is as though it breaks the consensus. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "I know of no disagreement that they were believers." As for the first reading, it does not support him, because people have answered that with several answers. Among them: that its meaning is "is it easy for you to ask your Lord?", as in your saying to another "Are you able to stand?" while you know that he is able to. Among them: that they asked him as one seeking information: does He send it down or not? If He sends it down, then ask Him for us.

Among them: that the meaning is: will He do that, and will there be from Him a response to that? From this is what was said to ʿAbd Allāh ibn Zayd: "Are you able to show me how the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to perform ablution?", i.e. would you like to? It was also said: the meaning is: does your Lord seek obedience through the sending down of the table? Abū Shāma said: "Similar to this in difficulty is what al-Haytham related — though it is weak — from Thābit from Anas: that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ visited Abū Ṭālib in an illness, and he said: 'O son of my brother, call upon your Lord whom you worship to cure me.' He said: 'O Allah, heal my uncle.' Abū Ṭālib got up as though released from a tether, and said: 'O son of my brother, your Lord whom you worship obeys you.' He said: 'And you, O uncle, if you obeyed Him' — or: 'if you obey Allah He will obey you', i.e. He will answer you in what you seek." I say: what made that acceptable is his ﷺ matching his uncle's wording, as in His words: {وَمَكَرُواْ وَمَكَرَ الله} [Āl ʿImrān: 54]. It was also said: the implied form is "does He obey?", the sīn being redundant (zāʾida), as in their saying استجاب and أجاب; he said:

184 - 4- وداعٍ دعا يا مَنْ يُجيب إلى النَّدى ... فلم يَسْتِجَبْه عند ذاك مُجيبُ
(Many a caller called: "O who will answer [the call] to generosity?" — yet no answerer answered him then.)

With these answers there is no need for the saying of one who said: "«يستطيع» is redundant", the meaning being "does your Lord send down", because no verb is made redundant except «كان», under two conditions; the redundancy of others is irregular, in places I have enumerated in a book other than this — although the Kufans permit the redundancy of some verbs absolutely; they related: «قَعَدَ فلانٌ يتهكَّم بي» (so-and-so sat mocking me), and they recited:

184 - 5- على ما قام يَشْتِمُني لئيمٌ ... كخنزيرٍ تَمَرَّغَ في رَمادِ
(Why does a base man stand reviling me, like a pig rolling in ashes?)

And the Basrans related, as irregular: «ما اصبحَ أبردَها وما أمسى أدفأَها» (how cold it is in the morning and how warm in the evening), meaning the world.

His words {أَن يُنَزِّلَ}: in the reading of the majority it is in the position of accusative as a mafʿūl bihi (direct object), i.e. the sending down. Abū al-Baqāʾ said: "The implied form is: «على أن ينزَّل» or «في أن ينزَّل»; and it is permissible that no preposition be needed, on the view that «يَسْتطيع» means «يُطيق» (is capable of)." I say: he only needed to assume the two prepositions in the first case because he took the ability to mean answering; as for his later saying "يستطيع means يُطيق", it is fully apparent only on al-Zamakhsharī's view that they were not believers. As for al-Kisāʾī's reading, they said: it is in the position of accusative as the object of the implied "asking", i.e. "are you able to ask your Lord for the sending down?"; so the implied maṣdar (verbal noun) is annexed to its first object, «ربّك», and when the maṣdar was omitted it became accusative. There is a point to consider in this, in that they made an implied maṣdar govern, which is not permissible according to the Basrans; they interpret whatever appears so outwardly. It is also permissible that «أن ينزَّل» be a badal ishtimāl (substitute of inclusion) from «ربك», the implied form being: "are you able", i.e. are you capable of, "Allah the Exalted's sending down a table by reason of your supplication?" This is a good aspect.

«مائدة» is the object of «يُنَزِّلُ». The مائدة is a table with food on it; if there is no food on it, it is not a مائدة. This is the well-known view; however, al-Rāghib said: "المائدة is the tray on which there is food, and each of them [i.e. the tray and the food] is called مائدة", which is contrary to what the majority hold. This question has parallels in the language: a table (خِوان) is not called مائدة unless there is food on it, otherwise it is خِوان; one does not say كأس unless there is wine in it, otherwise it is قَدَح; one does not say ذَنوب or سَجْل unless there is water in it, otherwise it is دَلْو (bucket); one does not say جِراب unless it is tanned, otherwise it is إهاب (raw hide); and not قَلَم unless it is sharpened, otherwise it is أنبوب (a reed tube).

The lexicographers differed about its derivation. Al-Zajjāj said: "It is from مادَ يَميدُ, when something moves; from it is His saying: {رَوَاسِيَ أَن تَمِيدَ بِهِمْ} [al-Anbiyāʾ: 31], and from it is مَيْدُ البحر (sea-sickness)", which is what afflicts one who rides it; so it is as though it sways with the food on it. He said: "It is فاعِلة in its original sense." Abū ʿUbayd said: "It is فاعِلة in the sense of مَفْعولة, derived from مادَهُ meaning 'he gave him', and امتادَهُ meaning 'he asked him to give'; so it means مَفْعولة", he said, "as in عِيشة راضِية (a pleasing life). Its origin is that its owner was given it (مِيدَ بها); the Arabs say: مادَني فلان يَميدني when he treats me well and gives to me." Abū Bakr ibn al-Anbārī said: "It was called مائدة because it is relief and a gift, from the Arabs' saying: مادَ فلانٌ فلاناً when he treats him well"; and he recited:

184 - 6- إلى أميرِ المؤمنين المُمْتادْ ...
(To the Commander of the Believers, the bountiful…)

i.e. the one who is good to his subjects. [On this view] it is فاعِلة from المَيْد in the sense of "giving", which is close to Abū ʿUbayd's view on the derivation, except that for him [Ibn al-Anbārī] it has the active sense of فاعِلة in its usual meaning. Ibn Qutayba agreed with Abū ʿUbayd that it means مفعولة, saying: "because the eaters are given it (يُمادُ بها)." It was also said: it is from المَيْد meaning inclining, and this is the meaning of al-Zajjāj's view. His words «من السماء» may be attached to (mutaʿalliq) the verb before it, or attached to an omitted [word] as a description of «مائدة», i.e. a table existing from heaven, i.e. descending from it.

semin-durr:113-113.t:
The majority read {ونَعْلَمَ} and «نكون» with the nūn of the first person, as active. Ibn Jubayr read — according to what Ibn ʿAṭiyya transmitted from him — «وتُعْلَم» with ḍamma on the tāʾ, as passive, the pronoun referring to the hearts, i.e. "and that our hearts be made to know". It is also transmitted from him «ونُعْلَم» with the nūn, as passive. And it was read «يُعْلم» with the yāʾ, as passive, what stands in place of the fāʿil (agent) being «أَنْ قد صدقتنا», i.e. "and that your truthfulness to us be known". It is not permissible in this reading for the verb to be predicated of the pronoun of the hearts, because it is treated like a figurative feminine, and the verb of its pronoun may not be made masculine. Al-Aʿmash read «وتَعْلَم» with a tāʾ, the verb being active, and its subject is the pronoun of the hearts; it is not permissible for the tāʾ to be of address, because the meaning would be corrupted. It was also related «وتِعْلَم» with kasra on the prefix of the imperfect, the meaning being as before. And it was read «وتَكون» with the tāʾ, the pronoun being for the hearts.

«أَنْ» in «أَنْ قد صَدَقْتَنا» is lightened [from أنّ], its noun being omitted, and «قد» is a separator because the clause occurring as its khabar (predicate) is verbal, with a fully inflected verb, and not a supplication; you have learned that from what preceded at His words: {أَلاَّ تَكُونَ فِتْنَةٌ} [al-Māʾida: 71]. «أن» and what follows it stand in place of the two objects, or in place of the first only, with the second omitted. «عليها» is attached to (mutaʿalliq) an omitted [word] indicated by «الشاهدين»; it is not attached to what follows it, because according to the majority what comes after «أل» does not govern what precedes it; those who permit that say: "It is attached to الشاهدين, fronted for the sake of the verse-endings." Al-Zamakhsharī permitted «عليها» to be a ḥāl (circumstantial), for he said: "or that we be among those who bear witness to Allah's oneness and to your prophethood, devoted to it (عاكفين عليها), on the view that «عليها» is in the position of a ḥāl." I say: his saying «عاكفين» is an interpretation of meaning, because in these places nothing is implied except general verbs of being. By what I have said, what the Shaykh said does not apply to him — for this escaped him — when he made it contradictory on the grounds that when he attached it to «عاكفين» it was not a ḥāl, since if it were a ḥāl it would be attached to a general verb of being. I do not know what the meaning of the contradiction is, nor how he could press against him to this extent.

The words of Allah the Exalted: {وَآيَةً}: conjoined to «عيداً», and «منك» is its description. Al-Yamānī read «وإنَّه» with the doubled «إنَّ», the pronoun being either for the feast (العيد) or for the sending down.

semin-durr:32-32.t:
His saying, Exalted is He: {مِنْ أَجْلِ ذلك}: there are two views on it. The more apparent of them: that it is attached to (mutaʿalliq) «كتبنا», and «ذلك» points to the killing. «الأجْل» originally means committing a crime; one says «أَجَلَ الأمر إجْلاً وأَجْلاً», with fatḥa and kasra on the hamza, when one committed it alone. Of this is the saying of Zuhayr:

171 - 9- وأهلِ خباءٍ صالحٍ ذاتُ بينِهم ... قد احتربوا في عاجلٍ أنا آجِلُهْ
(And the people of a tent whose mutual relations were good, who fought one another over a sudden matter that I had brought about)

i.e. "I am its perpetrator". The meaning of people's saying «فَعَلْتُه من أجْلِك ولأجلك» is: because of you, meaning: from your having brought about its doing and made it necessary. Likewise their saying «فَعَلْتُه من جَرَّائك» — its origin is "from my having dragged it", then it came to be used in the sense of cause; of this is the ḥadīth: «مِنْ جَرَّاي», i.e. because of me. «من» is for the beginning of the extent, i.e. the prescribing arose and began from the crime of killing. It is permissible to omit «مِنْ» and the lām and to make «أَجْل» accusative as a mafʿūl lahu (object of purpose) when it fulfils the conditions. He said:

172 - 0- أَجْلَ أنَّ اللهَ قد فَضَّلكمْ ... . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
(Because Allah has preferred you …)

The second — some people permitted it —: that it is attached to His saying «مِن النادمين», i.e. he regretted because of that, i.e. his killing his brother. Abū al-Baqāʾ said: "It is not attached to «النادمين», because it is not good to begin with «كتبنا» here." This rejection is not clear: where is the lack of goodness in beginning with that? Allah began by informing that He prescribed that, and the information is connected to the story of the two sons of Adam. However, the apparent view is otherwise, as has preceded.

The majority read with fatḥa on the hamza of «أجل», and Abū Jaʿfar read it with kasra, which is a dialect form as has preceded. It is also narrated from him that he dropped the hamza and threw its vowel, which is the kasra, onto the nūn of «من», just as Warsh transfers its fatḥa onto it. The hāʾ in «أنه» is the pronoun of the matter and the affair (ḍamīr al-amr wa-l-shaʾn). «مَنْ» is conditional and a mubtadaʾ (subject), and it [together with] its khabar (predicate) is in the position of the nominative as the khabar of «أنّ». [Translator's note: the source reads «وهي خبرُها»; «وهي وخبرُها» ("it and its khabar") is evidently meant.] His saying «بغير نفسٍ»: there are two views on it. One of them: that it is attached to the killing before it. The second: that it is in the position of a ḥāl (circumstantial) from the agent pronoun in «قَتَل», i.e. he killed it wrongfully; Abū al-Baqāʾ mentioned it.

His saying: {أَوْ فَسَادٍ}: the majority read it in the genitive, by conjunction with «نفس», which is genitive by the annexation of «غير» to it. Al-Ḥasan read it in the accusative, and there are two views on it. The more apparent of them: that it is accusative as a mafʿūl bihi (direct object) by an implied governor that suits the context, i.e. "or brought about — or did — corruption". The second: that it is a maṣdar (verbal noun), the implied form being «أو أَفْسَدَ فساداً» in the sense of «إفساداً», so it is a noun of the maṣdar (ism maṣdar), like the poet's saying:

172 - 1-. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ... وبعد عطائِكَ المئةَ الرِّتاعا
(… and after your giving the hundred grazing [camels])
